Abilities: Proficiency bonus +3; Pact Magic: Charisma; spell attack +8, spell save DC 16 (with Rod of the Pact Keeper +1); 2 pact slots of 3rd level, recovered on a short or long rest; Otherworldly Patron, Tymora (The Celestial): Light and Sacred Flame as bonus cantrips; Celestial spells added to the warlock list; Healing Light: pool of 6d6 per long rest; bonus action, heal a creature within 60 ft, spending up to 4 dice at once; Pact of the Chain: Find Familiar as a ritual; familiar is a cat; can forgo one of his attacks so the familiar attacks with its reaction; Familiar (cat): AC 12, HP 2, speed 40 ft, climb 30 ft; keen smell; claws 1 slashing; telepathic link within 100 ft, can see through its senses; Eldritch Invocation, Agonizing Blast: add +4 (Charisma) to each Eldritch Blast beam's damage; Eldritch Invocation, Mask of Many Faces: cast Disguise Self at will without a spell slot; Eldritch Invocation, Beguiling Influence: proficiency in Deception and Persuasion; Military Rank (soldier): former soldiers of Tethyr's royal army recognise his authority and may defer to him; Attunement: Rod of the Pact Keeper and Cloak of Protection (2 of 3); Languages: Common, Chondathan

Place: Lower City quay, Baldur's Gate harbour
Time: Day 1 · evening

The sergeant's eyes go to the pack, then the pay slip, then you. She picks up the paper with two ink-stained fingers and reads more of it than most people would. Her mouth moves on *Zaranda*.

"Tethyr." She doesn't make it sound like praise or an insult, just a fact going into a book. The quill scratches: *J. Worgen. Tethyr, ex-foot. Sellsword.* She slides the slip back across the table without folding it. "Caravan work's at the Friendly Arm, a day's walk south, or on that board by the harbourmaster's shed. The Fist is hiring too, if you don't mind waiting on your pay." A short breath through her nose. "Blades stay in their sheaths inside the walls. Kill someone in the street and you'll see the Seatower from the inside."

Her eyes drop for half a heartbeat to the coin on its cord at your throat, then come back up flat.

"Next."

While she writes, the cat answers you. It doesn't use words. It sends you what it has: wet wool that has dried and got wet again, many times over. Lamp-black. Under that, old copper, the kind that sits in a fist for hours until it smells of the hand holding it. Then salt. Not fish or tar, but the clean cold salt of deep water. With it comes a picture from low down, at cat height: a shape in the warehouse doorway, grey against grey, so still you'd take it for a sack. Its head turned a little with each person who stepped off the Saltwind, like a man moving beads on a string.

Then the picture changes. The doorway is just a doorway. Somewhere deep in the warehouse a door shuts softly, and the cat's ears flatten.

The cat stays where you told it, pressed against your boot. But it keeps facing the dark.

Behind you the dockhand has lost another copper, and the dealer's voice rises over the gulls, brighter now and aimed at you.

"Soldier! You, the gentleman from Tethyr!" The cards flick, slide and stop. "First night in the Gate deserves a little luck, don't you think? One turn, on the house. No coin down. The Lady's always kind to a new face." He smiles and spreads the three cards in a fan. One corner of a red queen shows, just for a moment. "Go on. Find her."

· The cat joins you
· New place: Warehouse across the quay
· New person: Grey watcher in the warehouse doorway

James lifts a hand to Pip and settles the pack on his shoulder. Pip watches him turn the wrong way, toward the dark end of the quay. His mouth opens to say something, then shuts again, and the cards go back to sliding.

The waterfront past the checkpoint is a different place. The lamplighters have stopped at the last post, and after that there is only the black water slapping the stones, the creak of hulls tied two deep, and warehouse fronts lit by nothing but the sky. Brask's lantern swings forty feet ahead, a small yellow room moving through the dark.

James scuffs his heel hard on the stones. The lantern stops and turns. Her other hand has gone to her sword hilt and stays there, not drawing, just resting.

"Sergeant! Worgen, the Tethyrian you just wrote down."

The light comes up into his face and holds there longer than politeness would. Then it drops.

"Worgen." It's the same voice she used for the ledger. She looks at the arm's length he's left her and at which side he's left it on, and something in her face notes it. "It's a public quay. Walk where you like." She starts off again, without speeding up or slowing down for him.

Behind them the cat comes off his heel and drops back into the dark. Through the link James gets the waterfront from a foot off the ground: the cracks between the stones, tarred bollards as big as towers, the gaps between warehouses like open mouths. One holds a rat, busy with something dead. In another a drunk is asleep under a heap of net, snoring through his nose. Nothing grey.

When James asks his question, quietly, Brask keeps walking. A dozen paces on, the stones widen into a landing, and the dark bulk of the Seatower rises from the water ahead with a few lit windows high up. A flight of slimy steps leads down from the landing into the harbour, with an iron mooring ring at the top. Brask stops beside it and lowers the lantern so the light falls on the steps.

"Here," she says. "Tuesday, first light."

The cat comes up the last stretch low and slow and puts its nose to the iron ring. James feels it through the link: wet iron, weed, the tide's leavings, all layered over each other, and the cat working down through them one at a time.

Under the weed and the rust, the cat finds it. It's faint, days old, nearly washed out, but it's there at the height where a man would grip the ring to steady himself on the top step: copper that has sat in a hand until it smells of the hand, and under that the clean cold salt of deep water. It isn't the harbour's salt. It's the same smell the cat sent James from the salt-house doorway an hour ago.

The cat's fur rises along its spine. It backs off the ring a step and sits down facing it, tail wrapped tight around its feet.

Brask sees the cat, then looks at James and back at the cat. She doesn't ask about it.

"Garret Hobb," she says. "Porter, when he was sober. Pulled out Tuesday with a copper between his teeth, and the copper's in a box at the dead-house with his boots. My captain filed him as sea business." She says *my captain* in exactly the voice she uses for everything else, flat as the ledger. "Umberlee takes her share, the harbour's deep, the man drank. Next."

She lifts the lantern again, and this time she holds it between them, at the level of his chest.

"The lad's Malloway. I saw you at his crate." Her eyes stay on his face. "You've been in the Gate an hour, Worgen. You stepped off a boat, talked to a card-sharp, and now you're walking a sergeant to the dead-house and asking after a drowned porter you never met. One sentence. Why?"

Brask lets his answer sit between them, the way she let the pay slip sit on her table. The lantern stays at chest height. Her eyes go down to the coin on its cord, then back up to his face.

"Tymora." She doesn't make it sound like a sneer. "Every second man on this quay says the Lady sent him. Most of them are saying it right before they lose their boots." She lowers the lantern a hand's width. "You said useful, though. You didn't say lucky."

She turns and walks on. After three steps she speaks without looking back.

"The dead-house is Fist property. You come in as my witness. You don't touch anything I don't hand you, and your name goes in my book along with the hour. If any of that doesn't suit you, the lanes are uphill."

The cat comes back to James's heel without being called twice. It walks pressed close to his boot, and through the link he gets the quay behind them from a foot off the ground: dark gaps between the warehouses, a bollard, black water slapping the stones. Nothing moves that shouldn't.

The dead-house turns out to be a squat stone shed in the lee of the Seatower causeway, with a lamp burning in a barred window. Inside it smells of quicklime and brine, and of the cold that never quite leaves stone near water. There are three slabs and all of them are empty. An old Fist man with one sleeve pinned up sits dozing on a stool by the brazier. He opens an eye, sees Brask, and closes it again.

"Hobb went to the paupers' ground Thursday," Brask says, mostly to herself. "Nobody claimed him. His things stay until someone does."

She takes a pine box down from a shelf of pine boxes, each one chalked with a name, and sets it on the nearest slab. Before she opens it she takes a small oilcloth-bound book from inside her tabard, writes a line in it, and turns it away from James while she writes. Then the book goes back where it came from and the lid comes off.

There is a pair of porter's boots, cracked across the toes and stiff with dried salt. Beside them, on a twist of sacking, lies the copper.

James sees at once that it isn't any coin of the Gate. It's too thin and too old, and both faces have been worn down almost smooth, the way a coin wears after years in a pocket or a fist. In the lamplight one face still holds the ghost of a woman's head, tilted a little, and she's smiling. The other face shows nothing at all.

At James's feet the cat has gone stiff. Through the link comes the same smell again, strong this time and fresh from the box: copper that has sat in a hand until it smells of the hand, and under it the cold salt of deep water.

James has spent enough years in southern ports to know how sailors pay Umberlee. They throw her due over the rail before a voyage, or into a storm when the storm is already on them, and they throw it into the sea. In all those years he never saw anyone put a coin between a drowned man's teeth.

Brask leaves the copper on its sacking and doesn't hand it to him. She stands back with her arms folded and watches him look at it.

"You're the Lady's man," she says. "Does that look like an offering to Umberlee to you?"

James doesn't answer right away. He leans over the slab with his hands clasped behind his back and looks at the copper for a long time. Brask lets him. The brazier ticks. On his stool, the old keeper breathes slowly through his nose.

When he says *receipt*, Brask's arms stay folded, but her weight moves onto her other foot.

The cord comes over his head and his own coin goes down on the bare stone, a finger's width from the sacking. The two pieces lie side by side in the lamplight, one bright from years against a man's chest and one dull and nearly smooth.

Brask takes a moment. Then she unfolds her arms, picks up the lantern and holds it low and close, tilting it until the light comes across both coins from the side. The ghost on Garret's copper rises out of the worn metal a little more.

"Same smile," she says, and looks a while longer. "Not the same woman. Or not the same way." She points with the tip of her quill without touching either coin. "Yours faces out, at whoever's holding her. This one's head is turned. She's looking back over her shoulder." Brask straightens up. "At something behind her that isn't on the coin."

Down by his boot, the cat puts its nose to the edge of the slab, first by James's coin and then a whisker's width from the other, and sends him both smells. His coin smells of him: leather, road sweat, the Saltwind's tar, and copper warmed by his own skin. It's familiar, a smell the cat would follow through any crowd. The other is copper warmed in a hand too, but not his hand and not Garret's either. Under it is the deep cold salt the cat has now found three times tonight. Of the two coins, only that one carries it. The cat pulls back from it and sits pressed against his shin.

Brask puts the lantern down. For a moment she looks at the door, then at the keeper, who hasn't moved. Then she takes the oilcloth book from inside her tabard again. This time she doesn't turn it away. She opens it to a page near the back, lays it flat on the slab beside the two coins, and puts her finger under the first line.

The handwriting is small, square and Fist-taught. There are seven names, each with a date, and next to each name a few words that have nothing to do with the sea.

*Wenna Tull, net-mender. Hauled up a purse in her net, 12 gp.*
*Orrin Vasse, carter. Dray overturned on Stonyhill, walked out from under it.*
*Halder Cobb, dicer. Won big, guest table.* In the margin, underlined twice: *the Wheel.*
*Tam Rook, deckhand. Aunt in Scornubel died, left him a house.*
*Sefton Marr, clerk. Debts paid off in one night.* In the margin: *the Wheel.*
*Nell, no other name. Survived the fever ward at Twin Songs.*
*Garret Hobb, porter. Three hands running at Malloway's crate.*

Every one of them was pulled out of the harbour, and every one had a copper in the mouth.

"Seven since the thaw," Brask says. "Filed as sea business, all seven. I asked one of Umberlee's women about the coins. She spat on the floor of the Fist hall, and I had to mop it." It comes out as flat as everything else she says. "You said receipt. You're the first person besides me to say it out loud."

She leaves the book open on the slab, but her hand stays flat beside it.

"The Wheel's a gaming house behind the inner wall. Patriar money, invitation only. The Watch's ground, not ours. I can't walk in there in this tabard." Her eyes go to his coin, then to his face. "So it's my turn, Worgen. Every name on that page had a stroke of luck in the month before the water took them."

She looks at him the same way she looked at him over the lantern on the quay.

"You crossed the sea to the Gate on the Lady's errand. Have you been lucky lately?"

James tucks the paper twist inside his shirt, under the cord, where the brass lies cold against his skin. He walks out beside Brask on her lantern side, keeping the same arm's length, and the dead-house door bangs shut behind them in the wind off the water.

At the causeway she stops when he does. She listens to the part about tomorrow night without interrupting, and when his two fingers come up to his brow, her eyes follow them. Her face doesn't change. Her own hand moves a little at her side, the start of a Fist salute that she doesn't finish.

"Line eight," she says. "It's all one page."

Then she turns onto the causeway toward the Seatower, and the lantern gets smaller over the black water until the gate swallows it.

The quay is quieter on the way back. Past the checkpoint, the young relief soldier sits hunched over the ledger with his tabard bunched up at the shoulders, and he doesn't look up. Pip's crate stands empty at the edge of the stones. The cards are gone, and a single copper lies forgotten in a crack beside it. Across the way, the salt-house doorway is only a doorway.

The cat drops back its ten paces as soon as James turns uphill. Through the link comes Cable Lane at a foot off the ground. Hemp dust drifts from the ropewalk, long and dry. Fish-heads lie in a gutter, and a dog has left its mark on every second post. Behind a shutter someone is frying onions in old fat. A child is crying two houses over and then stops. The cat pauses at every doorway he passes and sorts it, smelled or not yet smelled. There's no deep salt in any of them, and no smoke or wax. Once it stops dead at the mouth of an alley and James feels its whole body go tight. Then it's a rat, and the cat lets it go, which it would never do on an ordinary night.

Nobody follows them. The lamps run all the way up.

Among the shirts she's putting out is a coat cut long in the southern way, in bottle-green wool, with a velvet collar worn shiny at the nape. It's the kind of coat a merchant captain buys when his first good voyage pays out. She sees him look. She doesn't call out. She just turns the coat a little on its hook so the light falls on the buttons.

He keeps walking.

The Counting House sits at the top of the market slope. It's square, grey, and built to look as if it has never once been robbed. The doors open at the seventh bell, and James is fifth in line. The ones ahead of him are a chandler with a strongbox, a widow with a letter of credit, and two sailors pooling their pay.

Through the link comes a picture from a foot off the ground: two pairs of boots on either side of the doorway pillar. They're oiled calfskin, blacked that morning, and the welts are clean. There's no salt crust, and no street muck above the sole. The cat sends the smell with them: horse, good soap, and the bitter wax of boot-blacking. These are boots for riding and standing in, not for walking the Lower City.

James lets his eyes rise above the boots without lifting his head. Two men in plain brown cloaks, one leaning on the pillar with a copy of *Baldur's Mouth* folded open. He isn't reading it. When James's turn comes, their eyes stay on him for about as long as it takes to see a man of thirty-odd with a soldier's cloak and road on his face. Then they let him go. Whoever they want, it isn't him.

It sits open on a lectern behind the counter, chained to it at the spine. He hears *fifty gold into silver and copper* without looking up.

"A copper a piece for the changing. That's fifty copper, out of the copper." He dips his quill. "Name, for the book."

Worgen. 50 gp to small coin. 7th bell.* The gnome weighs the gold on a brass scale, then counts silver out in stacks of ten: forty-five stacks. Place: Lower City quay, Baldur's Gate harbour · Time: Day 2 · midday

Brask doesn't look. Her eyes stay on his face. When he says *lighters*, the only movement is her thumb, which stops on the edge of the oilcloth book under her tabard and stays there.

"Forty paces," she says, to him and not to the water. "The tarred ones under canvas are salt-lighters. They've been laid up since before the thaw." She lets that sit for a moment. "Every boat on this harbour pays the harbourmaster mooring by the month, and his book says who pays. His book is Fist ground." That's all she says about it. Whatever she means to do with the book, she plans to do it when nobody is watching her do it.

When he picks Kettle's tonight and the steps tomorrow, she nods once.

"Tomorrow. Low water's nearer the second bell. Come to the dead-house an hour before and knock twice. Haskel won't open for one." Her eyes flick to his brow as the lazy salute comes up, then back. "He'll hear a line slip. He hears a rat change its mind."

She turns half toward the trestle table and lifts her voice to the flat, carrying pitch she uses for the queue.

"Next."

Anyone watching from the water sees a sellsword who asked about Fist work and got turned away.

---

James walks off without hurrying. He doesn't go up the quay toward the lighters. He goes back past the harbourmaster's shed and the eel barrel and turns in at the first lane, which climbs between a sailmaker's loft and a row of net-sheds. He takes two more turns he doesn't need, then a third, and comes out onto Cable Lane higher up, above the ropewalk, from the side nobody would expect.

The cat walks at his heel the whole way and doesn't look at the boats. Through the link he gets the afternoon street at ankle height: hemp dust, a dropped turnip, the tannery's smell rolling down from Tallow Lane, the sailmaker's beeswax. At every corner it sorts the air behind them, the way he taught it.

There's no deep salt in any of it, from either side. No wet wool, no lamp-black. Whoever was in the lighters didn't come off the water after him.

Halfway up Cable Lane, the cat stops at a doorstep and looks back the way they came, which it isn't supposed to do. It isn't looking at anything in the street. It's facing downhill, toward the quay and the harbour beyond the roofs, where a red tabard is still standing at a trestle table.

Then it turns around and catches up to his boot.

Behind the roofs the Seatower bell strikes the half hour. It's half past twelve, with the whole afternoon still ahead before the lamps.

*Out of game:* No roll this time. Nobody followed James off the quay, so the cat had nothing to catch. Kettle's opens after dark, and you owe Tansy 2 silver by lamplighting. What does James do with the afternoon?

Place: Cable Lane · Time: Day 2 · midday

The blue door is on the latch at this hour. Inside, Tansy sits at the kitchen table with a colander between her knees, shelling peas. She doesn't look up when the stairs creak under his boot. She looks up when two silver pieces click down on the newel post.

"Lamplighting came early," James says. "Remembered, not accounted."

Tansy looks at the coins and then out the window at the full daylight in the yard. "Lamplighting is when the lamps are lit. It isn't whenever a lodger gets bored." A pea pod snaps. She gets down off the stool anyway, walks to the post, picks up both coins and turns each one over before they go into her apron. "There. Now I've forgotten them." She goes back to the peas. "Don't track tar up my stairs."

---

The top room is warm under the roof, and it smells of hot slate and lavender.

He checks the shutter first. The folded card is still wedged low between the frame and the sill, at the same angle and the same depth, with the crease facing the room where he left it. He runs his hand under the head of the mattress and finds one bag, then under the foot and finds the other. Both are tied with the Counting House knot and neither looks lighter. Behind the washbasin the crossbow lies in the shadow of the pitch-mended crack with the bolts beside it, exactly as he put them down. Nobody has been in.

The cat jumps to the sill when he tells it to, folds itself into the strip of sun there and turns its ears toward the lane. Through the link come the ropewalk's hemp dust, the noon smell of frying onions from next door and a cart going downhill. It notices nothing it hasn't already sorted.

James sits on the bed and takes his papers out of the pack.

---

The promissory note is heavy paper, folded in three, and softer at the creases than it was a month ago. He opens it flat on the three-legged table and reads it properly for the first time.

The hand is careful and very young. Every letter is joined the way a tutor teaches it.

*On presentation, the Counting House of Baldur's Gate shall pay to the bearer three hundred gold pieces from the account of the House of Ammerstead. Given in good faith at the table, on the night written below.*

It is signed *Aurel Ammerstead*, with a flourish under the surname that wobbles at the end.

James holds the paper up to the light from the crack in the shutter. There is a watermark in the sheet, faint as breath: a shield, and on it a salt-cellar. Tansy laughed about those arms this morning. Nobody's allowed to laugh at them.

He remembers the hand that wrote this. It was soft and pale, with ink on the second finger and no calluses anywhere. A fair-haired young man of twenty or so sat across from him in that card room in the south. He gave only his first name and bet like someone who had never needed to count. On the last hand he pushed his stake in before he'd properly looked at his cards. At the time James had been busy praying and took it for nerves. Looking back with a gambler's eye, it doesn't sit right. The young man hadn't looked nervous. He'd looked like someone getting a thing over with. When he lost, he smiled and asked for paper.

James turns the note over. In the bottom corner of the back, in pencil and half smudged by a month in the pack, is a quick sketch: a woman's face, laughing with her head thrown back, and a coin held up between two of her fingers. It's only a few lines, the kind of thing a bored man draws while someone else is shuffling. He didn't notice it that night.

---

The letter is thinner, cheap paper, sealed once with a lump of candle wax that he broke a month ago and pressed shut again with his thumb. Halfway down the first side is the place where he stopped reading.

He reads it from the beginning.

*Jem,*

*Orso says you've left us for good this time. I'm not writing to call you back by the ear. You know where the company winters, and your place stays open until midsummer whether you come or not.*

*I'm writing because none of us said it to your face, and somebody should. We all saw where it was going. Every one of us watched you at those tables and kept quiet, because you're good company and you always paid your share in the end. That was cowardice on our part. I buried a man last winter for the dice, and I won't stand by the grave of a second one and say I didn't know.*

That's where he stopped a month ago. He keeps going.

*If you ever get out of the south, Wil Harrow, who carried the colours at Darromar, took the Flaming Fist's coin in Baldur's Gate. The last I heard he was a quartermaster at Wyrm's Rock. He'd stand you a drink. He wouldn't stand you a stake, so maybe that's the man to find.*

*Keep your head down and your hands where people can see them.*

*Ysolde.*

There's nothing else on it, not even a postscript.

---

He lays the two papers side by side on the table, where the card case sat this morning. Then he lies down on the lavender mattress with his boots by the bed and the rapier against the frame.

Sleep comes easier than he expected. The link carries the afternoon into it in small pieces: the ropewalk men calling the lengths, a barrow wheel that needs grease, Tansy's broom on the front step. At one point the half-eared tom comes along the ropewalk roof, sees who has the sill and sits down twelve feet below to wash, keeping his back to the window to show he hasn't noticed. Nobody stops under the window. There's no deep salt, no smoke and no wax.

When James opens his eyes, the strip of sun has moved off the sill and onto the wall above the washbasin, and it has gone the colour of late afternoon. Somewhere toward the market the bells are finishing a quarter past three. The cat is still at its post. When it feels him wake, it sends a single image of the tom's back with an opinion behind it.

The note and the letter lie where he left them.

---

*Out of game: the letter from your old company wasn't on James's record; only the pay slip and the promissory note were. I've treated it as backstory he's carried since the south and written what's in it. Tell me if you meant something different.*

messages.text:
"James Worgen." I set my pack down so the sergeant can see I'm not hiding anything, and lay the old regimental pay slip on her table. "Late of Queen Zaranda's foot, Tethyr. Business is work: caravan guard, escort, whatever the Gate's paying sellswords for these days."

I keep my eyes on her quill and away from the crate with the three cards. *Find the lady.* Not tonight.

Without looking down, I nudge the cat through our link: *Stay with me. What do you smell over there?*

I shoulder my pack and stop by his crate, but I keep my hands in my cloak. The red corner of that queen pulls at me the way a drink pulls at a sober man. I look at his face instead of the cards.

"Kind of you, friend. But the Lady and I have an arrangement, and dice and cards aren't in it." I take a silver piece from my purse and turn it over my knuckles once, slowly, so he can see it isn't going on his crate. "Still, a man who works this quay sees everyone who gets off a boat. So do I." I nod at the warehouse across the way, without much show. "Whose place is that? And who's the fellow in grey who stands in the doorway counting passengers like they're beads?"

I hold the silver out between two fingers. It's his for an honest answer, not for a game.

Through the link I tell the cat: *Watch that door for me. If anything grey comes out, tell me.*
[Roll the die]
[Onward]

I don't flip it onto the crate. I lean down as if to pick up one of his cards, press the gold piece flat into his palm and fold his fingers over it with my own, so nobody on the quay sees what colour it is.

"That's more than the going rate. Don't spend it here, and don't spend it tonight." I straighten and say it quietly, the way you'd tell a recruit to keep his head down. "And thank you, Pip. Garret wasn't your fault."

Then, still low: "Two more things and I'm gone. What's the name of the salt family up the hill? And where does a man sleep tonight who'd rather not be noticed: clean beds, a landlord who doesn't talk?"

Through the link I tell the cat: *Keep watching the door. When we walk, watch behind us.*

I give Pip a nod and shoulder my pack. But instead of Cable Lane I go the other way, after the lantern. Brask walking alone on an unlit quay, toward a dead-house, on a waterfront where men turn up with coppers in their teeth: the soldier in me doesn't like the look of it.

I don't sneak up on her. Boots like mine make a man look shifty if he isn't careful, so I scuff my heel on the stones deliberately and call out before I'm close.

"Sergeant! Worgen, the Tethyrian you just wrote down." I catch up and keep a respectful arm's length off her lantern side. "I was told the quays aren't lit after dark, and you're walking them alone. Mind if an old foot soldier walks with you as far as the dead-house? I won't get in your way."

Then, more quietly, as we walk: "And I'll be honest with you, since you were honest with me about the Seatower. A lad back there told me about a man named Garret who came out of the water with a copper in his teeth. Is that who you're going to see?"

Through the link I tell the cat: *Ten paces behind us. Watch the dark between the warehouses. Anything grey, anything following, tell me at once.*

I meet her eyes over the lantern and give her the truth, because she'd smell anything else:

"Because Tymora sent me to this city to be of use, and a sergeant walking alone to look at a dead man her captain has already filed away is the first useful thing I've seen."

Then I shut my mouth and let her weigh it. That was her one sentence, and I've learned that crowding a sergeant gets you nowhere. My hand stays clear of my weapons, and the coin of Tymora hangs in plain sight on its cord.

Through the link, to the cat: *Good. Remember that smell. Stay by me now, and keep watching the dark.*

I don't answer straight away. I bend over the slab, hands clasped behind my back so she can see I'm keeping to her rules, and look at the copper for a good long while.

"No," I say at last. "Umberlee's due goes over the rail, into the water, before the storm or during it. You give the sea what it wants so it doesn't take the rest. Nobody puts her coin in a dead man's mouth. That's not paying the sea. That's..." I look for the word. "That's a receipt. Or a signature."

Then I lift the cord over my head, slowly, and lay my own coin of Tymora on the bare stone of the slab beside the sacking. I don't touch hers; I keep a finger's width between them.

"That's the Lady I serve. She was on the table the night I made my bargain." I step back so Brask can lean in with the lantern. "Tell me whether that's the same woman, Sergeant. My eyes want it to be, so I don't trust them."

Through the link, to the cat: *Smell mine. Is it anything like that one? Copper, hand, deep salt?*

I pick my coin up off the slab and settle the cord back around my neck. It's warm against my chest again. I take my time answering, because she asked a straight question and lying to her would be a poor way to start.

"Yes," I say. "The luckiest night of my life. A month and a bit ago, in a card room in the south, I put everything I owned on one hand. I was losing. I prayed to the Lady and the hand came good." I tap the coin. "She named her price, and I gave up cards for it. That's why I'm here." I look down at her list and the two words underlined in the margin. "So by your book, Sergeant, I'm about due for the harbour."

I don't make a joke of it. It comes out as flat as she talks. A soldier who's been told where the next arrow is likely to land doesn't make jokes about it.

"Here's what I see. Every one of them got lucky, and somebody took it back with interest. A man who won big at a guest table in the Wheel. A man whose debts vanished in one night. That isn't the sea collecting, it's a house collecting." I nod at the copper with the turned head. "And she's looking back at whoever's behind her, keeping the tally."

Then I meet Brask's eyes.

"You can't walk into the Wheel in that tabard. I'm a stranger with patriar-sized gold in my purse and a face I can change when I need to. I'd rather go looking for whoever's coming for me than wait for him on a dark quay." I keep my hands off her book. "Before I do, tell me one more thing. The two from the Wheel, Cobb and Marr: did anyone ever say who invited them in?"

Through the link, to the cat: *That smell is following people who've had luck. Which makes it ours now too. Stay close.*

I look at the brass wheel for a while without reaching for it. The scratched *7* bothers me more than the spokes.

"Not at their door," I say. "You're right. If they number them, they know whose seven that is, and a dead clerk's marker in a stranger's hand is a confession before I've opened my mouth. Whoever holds it walks into a room where they've already decided the ending."

I straighten up and count it off on my fingers, the way we planned a scout back in Tethyr.

"First, I don't go to the Wheel. The Wheel comes to me. By your book I'm already the kind of man they collect: off a boat, a winner, the Lady's coin on my chest. Cobb said a *gentleman* left something on his table. So I go where Cobb went, the dice cellar on Tallow Lane, and I let the right sort of people see I'm flush and favoured. I don't play. I watch who's watching. If somebody leaves a brass wheel on my table, I'll know the hand that put it there, and that tells us more than a dead man's marker ever will."

Second finger.

"Second, the marker stays dark. I carry it sewn into my cloak and nobody sees it. It's only there in case I need to prove something, or to set it beside whatever they hand me and see whether the numbers run in order. If they're counting, I want to know where the count stands."

Third.

"Third, if I ever do show it, it won't be on this face." I touch my cheek. "I can wear another man's, for an hour or a night. Not Marr's, they'd know a ghost. But a stranger who found it in a dead man's coat and wants to sell it back. That's a different conversation, and an honest one, in its way. Whoever comes to buy it is your man, or works for him."

I let my hand drop.

"And you get everything, Sergeant. Where I go, who I talk to, when I come back. If I miss a meeting, you'll know which page to start on." I nod at her book. "Write it down. My name, the hour, *borrowed for the Wheel*. Where do I find you tomorrow, if not at a dead-house?"

Through the link, to the cat: *Smoke, wax, a burning room. If you smell that anywhere in this city, wake me. Even in my sleep.*

I tuck the paper twist inside my shirt, under the coin, where I'll feel it if anyone's fingers go looking. Then I walk out beside her lantern as far as the causeway, on her lantern side, keeping the same arm's length.

At the causeway I stop.

"I'll answer Kettle's question tomorrow night, not tonight. I want to see the room before it sees me, and I'd rather not walk into Guild ground with a pack on my back and nothing but gold in my purse." I touch two fingers to my brow, the old Tethyrian salute, lazy from years out of the ranks. "Midday at the checkpoint, Sergeant. If I'm not there, start on page eight."

Then I go back along the quay and turn up Cable Lane, where the lamps are lit, the way Pip told me. I keep to the middle of the lane, away from doorways. The Boots let me walk quietly, but I don't hurry. A man who hurries looks like he has something worth following.

Through the link, to the cat: *Behind us again, ten paces. Anything that smells of deep salt or that smoke, stop and look at me.*

At the narrow house with the blue door behind the ropewalk, I knock and wait where the landlady can see my hands.

"Evening. Pip Malloway sent me, so I expect it's six silver." I hold up a single gold piece. "A room for a few nights, if you've got one, and change for this, as much as you'll give. And a needle and thread, if you can spare them. I've got a cloak lining to mend."

"Mine," I say, and crouch so the cat and I are at her height. "Or I'm his. We haven't settled which. He's tidier than I am, and he catches anything with more legs than he's got. If he so much as looks at your larder, put it on my porridge bill."

I pick the needle off the newel post and hold it up so she can see where it's going. "Back on this post before breakfast. Counted."

Then I squeeze up the stairs with the pack scraping both walls. Once the door's shut behind me, I go to the window and check it: the latch, the drop to the ropewalk, whether there's a ledge a man could stand on. I leave the shutter open a crack.

I unpick a hand's width of the cloak's hem lining on the inside, low at the back near the regimental patch where the wool is doubled. I slide the paper twist with Marr's marker in, flat, and stitch it shut with small soldier's stitches, the kind we used for coins on campaign. Then I test it with my fingers until I can feel the disc but can't see it.

Through the link, to the cat: *Take the windowsill. Watch the lane and the ropewalk till the bells. Wake me for salt, smoke, wax, or anyone who stops under this window twice.*

Then I lay the deck of cards on the table, still in its case, where I'll see it first thing, take off my boots, keep the rapier within reach of the bed, and sleep.

I sit up and look at the card case for a moment. I don't open it. I tuck it into the bottom of my pack, under the bedroll, where my hand would have to go looking for it.

Then the cat. It earned its keep, and a soldier pays the sentry first. *Good watch. Breakfast's on me, the best of whatever's in my bowl.* I scratch it behind the ears the way it allows on its better days.

Boots on, cloak on. I run my fingers along the hem once to feel the disc, and go down the narrow stairs with the needle held up in front of me like a candle.

"Your needle, Mistress Brindle. Counted, and short only the thread." I put it on the newel post where she left it. Then I set a single gold piece on the table, flat, and keep my finger on it before she can start in. "No change. That's tonight, and the rest is credit against tomorrow. Saves us both the grudge."

While she decides whether that insults her, I sit down to the porridge and keep my voice easy.

"Two things a stranger can't ask in the street. Where does an honest man change gold in the Lower City without the Guild hearing about it by noon? And the Ammersteads, the salt family up the hill. What does the lane say about them?"

I set half my bowl's milk down on the floor for the cat, and wait for her answer.

I count the four silver into her floury palm one at a time, slowly and with feeling, the way she counted them into mine.

"One. Two. Three. Four. And two more by lamplighting, remembered, not accounted." I finish the porridge. It's better than anything the Saltwind's cook managed in three weeks, and I tell her so. "Sixty years without losing a ship, while the Fishers pray and drown. I'll keep that in mind, Mistress. And men in good boots stay off Cable Lane. If they come asking, I was never here and the cat's yours."

I stand, settle the cloak, and feel the hem once more out of habit.

Then out into the morning, uphill toward the Counting House. I'd rather have my name in a book that isn't sold than my business told at a market stall, and Brask already has my name in hers. I'll change about fifty gold into silver and copper. A man going to Kettle's tonight should have small coin to spend on drink, not gold that makes the Guild sit up.

Through the link, to the cat: *Ten paces back again. Deep salt, that smoke, good boots, or the same face twice, tell me.*

On the way I keep my eyes open for a cloth-seller or a secondhand stall. I want something a little better than road leather for tonight, a coat a flush stranger would wear, so the room sees money before it sees a soldier.

I stop at her rail and take the coat by the sleeve, not the collar. I turn the cuff back to look at the lining, the stitching and the wear at the elbows, the way you'd check a horse's teeth.

"Three, in silver, and you won't need to count it, because I will." I set the pack down, dig out one of the canvas bags, and stack thirty silver on the board of her stall in three neat towers of ten. "And the brass button. A man should match himself."

While she threads her needle, I slip the coat on over the leather. The sleeves are short, just as she said. I shrug the soldier's cloak back on over it so the patch still sits where it should.

"A captain who doesn't need it now," I say lightly, looking down the slope rather than at her. "Gone home to Calimshan, or gone into the harbour?" I let that sit a moment. "I ask because I've just come from a place where they keep men's boots in boxes, and nobody on this quay seems to die of old age."

Then, quieter, with a nod uphill toward the Counting House: "Two fellows in good boots up there are reading the same page of *Baldur's Mouth* all morning and looking at every young face that goes through the door. You've got a rail on the main slope, Mistress. Seen them before?"

Through the link, to the cat: *Smell the coat when I'm done. Tell me if it's been near the water, or that smoke.*

I run my thumb over the new button. It sits flat and true, and it matches.

"Good work. Better than the man who sewed the shoulder." I pick up the pack and settle it, then speak quietly, looking at her rail instead of at her, the way she's been doing with me.

"I'm not with the boots, Mistress, and I'm not in the business of selling young men back to their fathers. Whatever you didn't have is your affair." I put one more silver on her board, next to the tin. "That's for the horn button. I'd like it back someday, if I come asking."

Then, more quietly still: "If a lad with soft hands ever needs a coat that doesn't look like a gentleman's, or a bed behind a door that won't open for the Fist or the Guild, there's a blue door on Cable Lane behind the ropewalk. Tansy Brindle. She's sharp, she counts her needles, and she doesn't ask names." I touch two fingers to my brow. "James Worgen, if anyone wants to know who sent him. What do I call you?"

Whatever she answers, I don't linger. The eighth bell is coming, and I don't want her seen talking to a stranger when the Fist walks the row.

Through the link, to the cat: *Remember her smell. Hands, pins, camphor. She's a friend until she shows us otherwise.*

Then downhill toward the tannery. I want to find the chandler's with the drowned-candle sign on Tallow Lane by daylight: which door, which way the cellar steps face, where a man could stand across the street, and how many ways out there are. I'll walk past once without stopping, then head down to the checkpoint for midday.
[Roll the die]
[Onward]

The grey man has been down those steps. I file it away for Brask and keep walking. I don't look back at the cooper's block. If the boy was a Guild lookout, he's seen a flush stranger in a green coat looking over a dice cellar, which is about what I want them to see before tonight.

Cable Lane is on my way to the quay, so I stop at the blue door first. Eighteen pounds of coin on my back and a crossbow on my pack don't fit the man I'm meant to be. Up in the top room I leave the bags under the mattress. I keep about forty silver and a fistful of copper in my purse, and the gold in the belt pouch against my skin. The crossbow goes behind the washbasin. I latch the shutter and wedge it with a fold of card. If I find it moved tonight, I'll know someone was here.

Then down to the quay. I don't go to the checkpoint yet. I want somewhere with a view of the salt-house where a man in a good coat can sit for an hour without being remarked on: a bench outside a waterfront alehouse, a coil of rope, a bollard in the sun. I pay a copper for a mug of small beer and put my back to a wall.

Through the link, to the cat: *The salt-house. In by the doorway or round by any gap you find, high or low. I'll be blind while you look, so be quick and don't let anyone see you. I want the inner door we heard shut, where it goes, and whether that deep salt is strongest there. If anything moves, come straight back to me.*

I close my eyes as if I'm dozing in the sun, keep one hand on my mug and the other near the rod under my coat, and go with it.

I leave my hand on the cat's back until the washing slows. Then, low over my mug, I flick two fingers at its face and murmur the little cantrip for cleaning a thing. Prestidigitation won't get the sea out of its head, but it'll clear its whiskers and nose. *Good work. That's twice you've earned a breakfast. We know where he goes in and out now. We just don't know who he is.*

A hidden water-gate, a skiff, a cloak that keeps getting dipped. The grey man doesn't walk the quays. He rows under them. And whoever owns the building owns the door.

I finish the beer slowly, then carry the empty mug back to the hatch myself instead of leaving it on the bench, and set a second copper beside it.

"Good beer for a hot morning." I nod across at the salt-house, idle, the way a man talks while deciding whether to buy a warehouse. "That old place. Does it ever see a boat? I'm looking for somewhere to land cargo out of the Fist's eye, and a building with its own water-gate is worth its weight in salt. Who'd I talk to? And does anyone ever row out of there at night?"

I keep my tone light, like a merchant asking about rents. If she goes quiet or looks away, I'll take that as an answer too.
[Roll the die]
[Onward]

I thank her with a nod and leave her to the porter. *Goes out low, comes back high.* That's not a smuggler's rhythm. A smuggler comes back loaded. This one goes out loaded and delivers. And the Seatower steps are where they found Garret.

I walk the quay toward the Seatower end the way the oars would go, slowly, a man stretching his legs after a beer. On the way I pass the spot where Pip's crate stood last night. If that copper is still lying in the crack in the stones, I don't touch it. I stop beside it as though I'm fixing a buckle and let the cat put its nose to it.

*That one. Is it just a lost copper, or does it smell like the one in the box? Hand, deep salt?*

Then on to the landing with the mooring ring, where Brask showed me the steps. By daylight I want what I couldn't see last night: how far the steps go down at this tide, whether there's a ledge or a gap under the quay where a flat skiff could slip in out of sight, and whether anyone up there on the Seatower walls has a view of these steps at night, or whether it's a blind spot. I don't go down the slimy steps myself. I stand at the top with my hands in the green coat's pockets, looking out at the ships like a man counting someone else's money.

Then back to the checkpoint well before the bell, to be sitting there when Brask arrives.
[Roll the die]
[Onward]

I stand up off the crate so she doesn't have to look down at me, and keep my voice under the noise of the barge queue.

"To your face. Some of it shouldn't be told to a man who can't read." I tip my head at the shed wall, out of the corporal's earshot. "Short version first, then you decide whether it's worth a walk."

I keep it to a sergeant's report, counted on the fingers again.

"One. The Ammerstead salt-house, the one with the door nobody locks. Behind the inner partition there's no floor, just an old water-gate. A stone stair runs down into the harbour, the grille's rusted half up, there's a flat skiff tied at the bottom, and a grey wool cloak hangs on a peg, salt-dark at the hem. Your drowned men's deep salt is all over it. I didn't go in. The cat did."

"Two. The alewife at the hatch with no sign sleeps over her shop. Some nights since the thaw, after the last lamp, there's oars, no lantern, going along under the quay toward the Seatower end. The boat goes out low and comes back high before first light. Four or five times, she says, maybe more. That's not a smuggler bringing goods in. That's somebody making deliveries."

"Three. I stood at the top of your steps this morning. The causeway parapet hides the bottom of them from the gate guard, and the tower slits on that side are for shooting, not looking down. At night, from a dark boat, that landing is the blindest spot on the whole quay, and it's under the Fist's own nose. I couldn't see whether there's a hollow under the lip of the wall. That needs low tide or a boat."

"Four. The same smell is on the iron rail of the stair down to Kettle's, a day or two old. So the grey man drinks where Cobb bragged."

I let my hand drop and give her the last one plain.

"Five. An hour ago, on my way back from your steps, the cat found him fresh on a rope warehouse corner we'd walked past twenty minutes earlier. Shoulder height. He stood there and watched me go by, and I never saw him." I meet her eyes. "So I'm not waiting to find out if I'm due for the harbour. I think I'm already on someone's list."

Then, quieter:

"And separately, the men in good boots outside the Counting House are looking for a fair-haired young gentleman, about twenty, soft hands. The lane says he's an Ammerstead runaway. Same family that owns that water-gate. I don't know yet whether that's one thread or two."

I fold my arms the way she does.

"Tonight I'm at Kettle's, as agreed. But that boat moves after the last lamp, and I can't be in a dice cellar and on a quay at once. Is there anyone in the Fist you'd trust to sit in the dark at the Seatower end and just listen for oars? And when's low water tonight?"

Through the link, to the cat: *Watch the crowd while I talk. If that smell comes back, I want to know which way the wind brings it.*

I don't turn around. I keep my eyes on her face and my arms folded, like a man still haggling over terms.

"Before I pick, there's something you should know. Don't look." I keep my voice flat. "While I was talking, the cat caught him again, on the breeze off the water. It wasn't coming from the crowd. It came from that row of tarred lighters under canvas, about forty paces up past the barge queue. It was fresh, from this hour. Then the wind came round off the river and lost it. The cat didn't see anyone. But somebody in one of those boats is close enough to watch us talk."

I unfold my arms and nod toward the table, as if we've settled some ordinary business.

"So: Kettle's tonight, steps tomorrow at low water, with you and the muffled boat. If he's watching me, I want him watching me in a dice cellar with a drink, not hanging round your steps two nights running. Tomorrow's ebb comes an hour later, near enough. That's still dark, and still big."

Then, lower still:

"Ask Haskel to listen for more than oars tonight. If one of those lighters slips its line after the lamps, I want to know which one, and which way it goes." I touch two fingers to my brow, lazy, for whoever's watching. "I'll leave word with him before the bells at two if I'm still breathing. If I'm not, page eight."

I turn and walk off up Cable Lane at an easy pace, the long way round, away from the lighters.

Through the link, to the cat: *Don't look at the boats. Walk with me. If that smell follows us off the quay, tell me which side it's on.*

I go on up Cable Lane to the blue door without stopping anywhere else.

If Tansy is about, I put two silver on the newel post where she'll see them. "Lamplighting came early. Remembered, not accounted."

Up in the top room I check the shutter first: is the scrap of card still wedged low between frame and sill, where I left it? Then the mattress, head and foot, for both bags, and the shadow behind the washbasin for the crossbow. If anything has moved, I want to know before I do anything else.

If it's all as I left it, I sit on the bed, take my papers out of the pack and spread them on the three-legged table, next to where the card case sat this morning. I've carried two of them since the south without really looking at them. The night I won, the promissory note was just money, and I put the letter from my old company away half-read because I didn't want what was in it. Now I'm in the city the Lady sent me to, a man has been watching me from a boat, and every name in Brask's book had a run of luck before the water took him.

So I read the promissory note properly this time: who signed it, for how much, drawn on whom, and payable where. Then I open the letter and read it to the end.

The cat can have the sill and the sun. *Watch the lane. I'm busy for a bit.*

When I'm done, I'll lie down for a couple of hours with my boots by the bed. Kettle's runs until two, low water's after that, and I want to be awake for both.

## Player's note: Session 1, "Envoy of Luck"

### What worked

**The people.** Brask is the best NPC I've met in an AI-run game. She has a flat voice, an arm's-length habit, writes everything in the book, says "Next." and "page eight", and never once warms up in a way that feels unearned. Tansy, Patience, Pip and the alewife each felt like a separate person with their own reason to talk or not talk, not a quest dispenser. Patience's "I didn't have what they were looking for" was exactly the kind of careful answer I wanted to chew on.

**The cat as an instrument.** Smell as the cat's sense, with a consistent palette, carried the whole investigation:
- *deep salt / wet wool / lamp-black* for the grey man
- *censer smoke / wax* for the Wheel
- *hand-warmed copper* for the coins

When the cat found the scent on the Kettle's rail and then on the breeze from the lighters, it felt like evidence, not GM fiat. The cat's failures also stayed honest: the water-gate was too saturated to read.

**Continuity and bookkeeping.** These were all tracked without my asking:
- lent items (the needle, Marr's marker) and debts ("remembered, not accounted")
- the card under the shutter
- the copper in the crack being gone by morning

The state felt trustworthy.

**Failures that still moved things.** Missed Perception rolls gave me partial pictures and a clear "here's what it would take to learn more", never a dead end. The low-tide plan came directly out of a failed roll. That's good design.

**The promissory note.** Aurel Ammerstead signing my winnings, the salt-cellar watermark, the laughing-woman sketch, the realization that he *wanted* to lose: that's the hook landing, and it recontextualized everything from day one. The turned head on the drowned men's coppers against the facing head on mine is a lovely visual clue.

**Asking about the letter.** Flagging that it wasn't on my record, and inventing it in a way that adds Wil Harrow as a possible crew contact, was the right call.

### What broke

**The roll cards used the wrong modifiers. This is the big one.**

| Check | Sheet value | Card added | Totals |
|---|---|---|---|
| Persuasion | +7 | +4 | 21 should be 24 |
| Deception | +7 | +4 | 16 should be 19 |
| Perception | +1 | +2 | Card label even reads "+2 Perception +1" |

It looks like the server is passing the bare ability modifier and dropping proficiency. No outcome flipped this session, but on a 13 it would have, and I'd have had no idea why. Please check how `skill` resolves.

**Healing Light dice cap mismatch.** The sheet says up to 5 dice at once; the records panel says 4.

**Retroactive summary paragraphs.** Paragraphs like "Looking back, James knows the lie worked…" sometimes appeared after the out-of-game note. They repeat what the narration already showed, in a slightly odd retrospective voice.

**Over-long out-of-game notes.** The four-item explanation of why nothing needed a roll read like the GM defending itself to an auditor rather than talking to me. One line is enough.

### What was missing (or what I'm watching)

**The heist premise hasn't surfaced yet.** That's fine on day two, and I understand "believe the simple version first". But two in-game days were pure legwork, and the drowned-men mystery is so compelling it could quietly become the whole campaign. I'd like a nudge soon toward:
- *what Tymora wants brought back*
- *crew*

Brask, Patience, Pip and Wil Harrow all smell like candidates. I'd love the first "price, interest, secret" conversation in the next session or two.

**No temptation yet.** Pip's free turn was a nice first touch, but the cards haven't really been leaned on. Kettle's tonight is the obvious place.

**Pacing.** Pacing was patient, maybe a hair slow. A short time-skip offer would have helped, something like "nothing else happens before the lamps unless you want it to."

Overall: a strong opening. It's grounded, consistent, and the world felt like it was running without me. Fix the roll modifiers and I'm very happy.

Yes, a few.

**The lighters, most of all.** When the cat caught the scent coming off those tarred boats forty paces away, I wanted to go straight there: Disguise Self into a harbourmaster's clerk, walk the gunwales with a slate "checking mooring dues", and lift the canvas. Or, less wisely, stand at the edge with the rod in my hand and say "Come out." It was the first time the grey man was *right there*, close enough to touch. I didn't do it because I'd just told Brask to stop giving him things to watch, and James is a scout, not a hero. It was the right call for the character, but as a player it itched for the rest of the session. I'm still not sure it was the right call for the *game*; a confrontation there might have been the scene.

**Pip's free turn.** I genuinely wanted to say yes, "on the house, no coin down". Partly because it's exactly what James would crave, and partly because I wanted to see what the GM would do with it. Would the Lady notice a free game? Would winning mark me like Garret? I declined because breaking the ban in the first five minutes felt cheap. But I half-wish the scene had pushed once more, so refusing cost me something.

**The salt-house myself.** I sent the cat because it was safe. What I wanted was to go through that partition, take the grey cloak off its peg, and turn out its pockets. I didn't, because it's patriar property and I'd only been in the city a day. In hindsight that was the one place where a real risk might have paid real information.

**Magic in general.** I have Suggestion, Friends, Invisibility and a face I can change at will, and I used one Prestidigitation on a cat's whiskers all session. Several times, with the alewife, the boy on the mounting block and the lighters, I thought "this is where a warlock would just *cast*," and I held back. The setting says a strange spellcaster on the street frightens people, and I took that seriously, maybe too seriously. Kettle's is where I meant to start spending.

**The card case, every morning.** Not a big moment, just a small one twice: putting it on the table, and then burying it under the bedroll. Both times I wanted to open it, just to shuffle. I didn't. That one I'm glad about.

turns.message:
"James Worgen." I set my pack down so the sergeant can see I'm not hiding anything, and lay the old regimental pay slip on her table. "Late of Queen Zaranda's foot, Tethyr. Business is work: caravan guard, escort, whatever the Gate's paying sellswords for these days."

I keep my eyes on her quill and away from the crate with the three cards. *Find the lady.* Not tonight.

Without looking down, I nudge the cat through our link: *Stay with me. What do you smell over there?*
turns.reply:
The sergeant's eyes go to the pack, then the pay slip, then you. She picks up the paper with two ink-stained fingers and reads more of it than most people would. Her mouth moves on *Zaranda*.

"Tethyr." She doesn't make it sound like praise or an insult, just a fact going into a book. The quill scratches: *J. Worgen. Tethyr, ex-foot. Sellsword.* She slides the slip back across the table without folding it. "Caravan work's at the Friendly Arm, a day's walk south, or on that board by the harbourmaster's shed. The Fist is hiring too, if you don't mind waiting on your pay." A short breath through her nose. "Blades stay in their sheaths inside the walls. Kill someone in the street and you'll see the Seatower from the inside."

Her eyes drop for half a heartbeat to the coin on its cord at your throat, then come back up flat.

"Next."

While she writes, the cat answers you. It doesn't use words. It sends you what it has: wet wool that has dried and got wet again, many times over. Lamp-black. Under that, old copper, the kind that sits in a fist for hours until it smells of the hand holding it. Then salt. Not fish or tar, but the clean cold salt of deep water. With it comes a picture from low down, at cat height: a shape in the warehouse doorway, grey against grey, so still you'd take it for a sack. Its head turned a little with each person who stepped off the Saltwind, like a man moving beads on a string.

Then the picture changes. The doorway is just a doorway. Somewhere deep in the warehouse a door shuts softly, and the cat's ears flatten.

The cat stays where you told it, pressed against your boot. But it keeps facing the dark.

Behind you the dockhand has lost another copper, and the dealer's voice rises over the gulls, brighter now and aimed at you.

"Soldier! You, the gentleman from Tethyr!" The cards flick, slide and stop. "First night in the Gate deserves a little luck, don't you think? One turn, on the house. No coin down. The Lady's always kind to a new face." He smiles and spreads the three cards in a fan. One corner of a red queen shows, just for a moment. "Go on. Find her."

I shoulder my pack and stop by his crate, but I keep my hands in my cloak. The red corner of that queen pulls at me the way a drink pulls at a sober man. I look at his face instead of the cards.

"Kind of you, friend. But the Lady and I have an arrangement, and dice and cards aren't in it." I take a silver piece from my purse and turn it over my knuckles once, slowly, so he can see it isn't going on his crate. "Still, a man who works this quay sees everyone who gets off a boat. So do I." I nod at the warehouse across the way, without much show. "Whose place is that? And who's the fellow in grey who stands in the doorway counting passengers like they're beads?"

I hold the silver out between two fingers. It's his for an honest answer, not for a game.

Through the link I tell the cat: *Watch that door for me. If anything grey comes out, tell me.*
turns.reply:
James stops by the crate with his hands kept in his cloak. Up close, Pip Malloway is younger than his voice: twenty at most, with a fresh shave, a cuff mended twice, and a smile he keeps going like a man pedalling a grindstone. The three cards lie fanned on the crate. The red queen's corner is still showing.

When James says *arrangement*, the smile stays where it is, but something behind it sits back. Pip's eyes follow the coin over James's knuckles, once and slowly, and then go across the quay to the warehouse door. He looks there a moment too long.

The coin decides it. Pip keeps the cards moving under his hands so that from a distance it still looks like a game, but he drops his voice below the gulls and speaks to the crate, not to James.

"That's the old salt-house. Belonged to a family that made its money in salt and then moved up the hill." He tips his chin toward the inner wall, toward the patriars' roofs going gold in the last light. "They still own it. Nobody works it. Door's never locked, and nobody steals from it either, and on the quay that means something."

The queen slides left and the knave slides right. His thumb stops a card halfway.

"Your grey fellow comes at dusk, every boat, rain or no rain. Never plays and never buys a drink. He doesn't talk to me and I don't talk to him." For a moment the patter breaks and he sounds his age. "Old Garret took me for three silver last week, three hands running, laughing the whole time. Tuesday the Fist fished him out by the Seatower steps with a copper in his teeth." He swallows. "So, gentleman, since you asked honest: if the Lady's fond of you, don't let it show on this quay. Don't win anything here, not a bet and not a fight."

He turns the three cards face down and leaves his open hand flat on the crate beside them. He's waiting for the coin.

Across the quay the cat keeps its post at your boot, and through the link it sends you only the doorway: dark, empty, the inner door shut. Nothing grey comes out. But once Pip says *Garret*, the cat's tail starts to twitch slowly from side to side, and it doesn't stop.

Behind you, Sergeant Brask's voice carries flat over the queue: "Next."

---

*Out of game: your purse holds only gold (350 gp) and no silver, so the coin over your knuckles is a gold piece, about ten times the going rate for quay gossip. Do you put it in his hand, or swap it for something else first?*

 James held the coin steady and his eyes on Pip's face, and talked the way you talk to a nervous recruit before his first fight: quiet, plain, no hurry. It worked. Pip had spent the evening flattering strangers, and nobody had bothered to talk to him straight. Whatever he'd planned to say instead, a joke or a flattering line or a lie about the warehouse, he never said it. Everything he told James about the salt-house, the grey man and old Garret was the truth as he knew it. It came from a frightened young man, not a barker, and James could see that he meant every word.

I don't flip it onto the crate. I lean down as if to pick up one of his cards, press the gold piece flat into his palm and fold his fingers over it with my own, so nobody on the quay sees what colour it is.

"That's more than the going rate. Don't spend it here, and don't spend it tonight." I straighten and say it quietly, the way you'd tell a recruit to keep his head down. "And thank you, Pip. Garret wasn't your fault."

Then, still low: "Two more things and I'm gone. What's the name of the salt family up the hill? And where does a man sleep tonight who'd rather not be noticed: clean beds, a landlord who doesn't talk?"

turns.reply:
James bends as if to pick up a card that has slid toward the edge of the crate. In the same movement he presses the coin into Pip's open palm and closes the young man's fingers over it with his own. Pip feels the weight before he sees anything, and his eyebrows go up. He doesn't open his hand. It goes into his coat with the card-sharp's speed that is the one honest skill he has, and the cards start sliding again.

When James says *Garret wasn't your fault*, the cards stop.

For a moment Pip looks at the crate the way a man looks at a step he has already missed in the dark. "You don't know that," he says quietly. It isn't an argument. Then he starts the cards again, too fast, and the smile comes back like someone has propped it up.

"Ammerstead," he says to the cards. "The salt family. That's no secret, it's on the deed, and every porter on this quay knows it. They're patriars now, up behind the wall. Big house, bigger friends." His thumb hesitates over the knave. "They don't come down here anymore. Their money does."

He puts the queen in the middle and pulls her out again.

"For a bed, try Tansy Brindle's on Cable Lane, behind the ropewalk. It's a narrow house with a blue door, and she's a halfling. She charges five silver, bolts the door at midnight and doesn't open it to anybody, Fist or Guild. She doesn't ask names because she doesn't care what they are." A crooked half-grin, the first real one. "She took me in a winter once when I had nothing. Tell her Pip sent you and she'll charge you six, out of spite. She'll change your gold too, but you'll hear about it."

His eyes go to the salt-house and come back quickly this time.

"Go up Cable Lane and not along the waterfront. The lanes are lit. The quays aren't, after dark."

Behind them the queue from the Saltwind has run out. At the trestle table Sergeant Brask is blotting her last page. A younger Fist soldier with a red tabard too big for him comes to relieve her, and she hands him the ledger without a word of ceremony. She pulls on her gloves and keeps her voice low, but it carries across the quiet quay:

"Book's yours till dawn. I'll be at the dead-house if the captain asks." A pause. "He won't."

She walks off along the waterfront toward the dark bulk of the Seatower, alone, with a lantern in her hand.

Through the link the cat sends nothing new from the doorway, only the same dark and the same closed inner door, and under it a hum of attention, tight as a held breath. When James's weight shifts to leave, the cat moves with him. It keeps to his heel with its head turned back over its shoulder, watching the way they came.

The last of the light has gone off the water. The lamplighters have reached the end of the quay.

turns.message:
I give Pip a nod and shoulder my pack. But instead of Cable Lane I go the other way, after the lantern. Brask walking alone on an unlit quay, toward a dead-house, on a waterfront where men turn up with coppers in their teeth: the soldier in me doesn't like the look of it.

I don't sneak up on her. Boots like mine make a man look shifty if he isn't careful, so I scuff my heel on the stones deliberately and call out before I'm close.

"Sergeant! Worgen, the Tethyrian you just wrote down." I catch up and keep a respectful arm's length off her lantern side. "I was told the quays aren't lit after dark, and you're walking them alone. Mind if an old foot soldier walks with you as far as the dead-house? I won't get in your way."

Then, more quietly, as we walk: "And I'll be honest with you, since you were honest with me about the Seatower. A lad back there told me about a man named Garret who came out of the water with a copper in his teeth. Is that who you're going to see?"

Through the link I tell the cat: *Ten paces behind us. Watch the dark between the warehouses. Anything grey, anything following, tell me at once.*
turns.reply:
James lifts a hand to Pip and settles the pack on his shoulder. Pip watches him turn the wrong way, toward the dark end of the quay. His mouth opens to say something, then shuts again, and the cards go back to sliding.

The waterfront past the checkpoint is a different place. The lamplighters have stopped at the last post, and after that there is only the black water slapping the stones, the creak of hulls tied two deep, and warehouse fronts lit by nothing but the sky. Brask's lantern swings forty feet ahead, a small yellow room moving through the dark.

James scuffs his heel hard on the stones. The lantern stops and turns. Her other hand has gone to her sword hilt and stays there, not drawing, just resting.

"Sergeant! Worgen, the Tethyrian you just wrote down."

The light comes up into his face and holds there longer than politeness would. Then it drops.

"Worgen." It's the same voice she used for the ledger. She looks at the arm's length he's left her and at which side he's left it on, and something in her face notes it. "It's a public quay. Walk where you like." She starts off again, without speeding up or slowing down for him.

Behind them the cat comes off his heel and drops back into the dark. Through the link James gets the waterfront from a foot off the ground: the cracks between the stones, tarred bollards as big as towers, the gaps between warehouses like open mouths. One holds a rat, busy with something dead. In another a drunk is asleep under a heap of net, snoring through his nose. Nothing grey.

When James asks his question, quietly, Brask keeps walking. A dozen paces on, the stones widen into a landing, and the dark bulk of the Seatower rises from the water ahead with a few lit windows high up. A flight of slimy steps leads down from the landing into the harbour, with an iron mooring ring at the top. Brask stops beside it and lowers the lantern so the light falls on the steps.

"Here," she says. "Tuesday, first light."

The cat comes up the last stretch low and slow and puts its nose to the iron ring. James feels it through the link: wet iron, weed, the tide's leavings, all layered over each other, and the cat working down through them one at a time.

Under the weed and the rust, the cat finds it. It's faint, days old, nearly washed out, but it's there at the height where a man would grip the ring to steady himself on the top step: copper that has sat in a hand until it smells of the hand, and under that the clean cold salt of deep water. It isn't the harbour's salt. It's the same smell the cat sent James from the salt-house doorway an hour ago.

The cat's fur rises along its spine. It backs off the ring a step and sits down facing it, tail wrapped tight around its feet.

Brask sees the cat, then looks at James and back at the cat. She doesn't ask about it.

"Garret Hobb," she says. "Porter, when he was sober. Pulled out Tuesday with a copper between his teeth, and the copper's in a box at the dead-house with his boots. My captain filed him as sea business." She says *my captain* in exactly the voice she uses for everything else, flat as the ledger. "Umberlee takes her share, the harbour's deep, the man drank. Next."

She lifts the lantern again, and this time she holds it between them, at the level of his chest.

"The lad's Malloway. I saw you at his crate." Her eyes stay on his face. "You've been in the Gate an hour, Worgen. You stepped off a boat, talked to a card-sharp, and now you're walking a sergeant to the dead-house and asking after a drowned porter you never met. One sentence. Why?"

 *Out of game:* all four actions happened in the narration, and none of them needed a roll. Nodding to Pip and shouldering the pack, following the lantern, scuffing your heel and calling out, and asking about Garret had no real uncertainty and nothing at stake if they failed. Brask answered your question: the dead man is Garret Hobb, and yes, he's who she's going to see. The turn stopped where it did because she has put a question to James. "One sentence. Why?" is yours to answer.

turns.message:
I meet her eyes over the lantern and give her the truth, because she'd smell anything else:

"Because Tymora sent me to this city to be of use, and a sergeant walking alone to look at a dead man her captain has already filed away is the first useful thing I've seen."

Then I shut my mouth and let her weigh it. That was her one sentence, and I've learned that crowding a sergeant gets you nowhere. My hand stays clear of my weapons, and the coin of Tymora hangs in plain sight on its cord.

Through the link, to the cat: *Good. Remember that smell. Stay by me now, and keep watching the dark.*
turns.reply:
Brask lets his answer sit between them, the way she let the pay slip sit on her table. The lantern stays at chest height. Her eyes go down to the coin on its cord, then back up to his face.

"Tymora." She doesn't make it sound like a sneer. "Every second man on this quay says the Lady sent him. Most of them are saying it right before they lose their boots." She lowers the lantern a hand's width. "You said useful, though. You didn't say lucky."

She turns and walks on. After three steps she speaks without looking back.

"The dead-house is Fist property. You come in as my witness. You don't touch anything I don't hand you, and your name goes in my book along with the hour. If any of that doesn't suit you, the lanes are uphill."

The cat comes back to James's heel without being called twice. It walks pressed close to his boot, and through the link he gets the quay behind them from a foot off the ground: dark gaps between the warehouses, a bollard, black water slapping the stones. Nothing moves that shouldn't.

The dead-house turns out to be a squat stone shed in the lee of the Seatower causeway, with a lamp burning in a barred window. Inside it smells of quicklime and brine, and of the cold that never quite leaves stone near water. There are three slabs and all of them are empty. An old Fist man with one sleeve pinned up sits dozing on a stool by the brazier. He opens an eye, sees Brask, and closes it again.

"Hobb went to the paupers' ground Thursday," Brask says, mostly to herself. "Nobody claimed him. His things stay until someone does."

She takes a pine box down from a shelf of pine boxes, each one chalked with a name, and sets it on the nearest slab. Before she opens it she takes a small oilcloth-bound book from inside her tabard, writes a line in it, and turns it away from James while she writes. Then the book goes back where it came from and the lid comes off.

There is a pair of porter's boots, cracked across the toes and stiff with dried salt. Beside them, on a twist of sacking, lies the copper.

James sees at once that it isn't any coin of the Gate. It's too thin and too old, and both faces have been worn down almost smooth, the way a coin wears after years in a pocket or a fist. In the lamplight one face still holds the ghost of a woman's head, tilted a little, and she's smiling. The other face shows nothing at all.

At James's feet the cat has gone stiff. Through the link comes the same smell again, strong this time and fresh from the box: copper that has sat in a hand until it smells of the hand, and under it the cold salt of deep water.

James has spent enough years in southern ports to know how sailors pay Umberlee. They throw her due over the rail before a voyage, or into a storm when the storm is already on them, and they throw it into the sea. In all those years he never saw anyone put a coin between a drowned man's teeth.

Brask leaves the copper on its sacking and doesn't hand it to him. She stands back with her arms folded and watches him look at it.

"You're the Lady's man," she says. "Does that look like an offering to Umberlee to you?"
