turns.message:
I don't answer straight away. I bend over the slab, hands clasped behind my back so she can see I'm keeping to her rules, and look at the copper for a good long while.

"No," I say at last. "Umberlee's due goes over the rail, into the water, before the storm or during it. You give the sea what it wants so it doesn't take the rest. Nobody puts her coin in a dead man's mouth. That's not paying the sea. That's..." I look for the word. "That's a receipt. Or a signature."

Then I lift the cord over my head, slowly, and lay my own coin of Tymora on the bare stone of the slab beside the sacking. I don't touch hers; I keep a finger's width between them.

"That's the Lady I serve. She was on the table the night I made my bargain." I step back so Brask can lean in with the lantern. "Tell me whether that's the same woman, Sergeant. My eyes want it to be, so I don't trust them."

Through the link, to the cat: *Smell mine. Is it anything like that one? Copper, hand, deep salt?*
turns.reply:
James doesn't answer right away. He leans over the slab with his hands clasped behind his back and looks at the copper for a long time. Brask lets him. The brazier ticks. On his stool, the old keeper breathes slowly through his nose.

When he says *receipt*, Brask's arms stay folded, but her weight moves onto her other foot.

The cord comes over his head and his own coin goes down on the bare stone, a finger's width from the sacking. The two pieces lie side by side in the lamplight, one bright from years against a man's chest and one dull and nearly smooth.

Brask takes a moment. Then she unfolds her arms, picks up the lantern and holds it low and close, tilting it until the light comes across both coins from the side. The ghost on Garret's copper rises out of the worn metal a little more.

"Same smile," she says, and looks a while longer. "Not the same woman. Or not the same way." She points with the tip of her quill without touching either coin. "Yours faces out, at whoever's holding her. This one's head is turned. She's looking back over her shoulder." Brask straightens up. "At something behind her that isn't on the coin."

Down by his boot, the cat puts its nose to the edge of the slab, first by James's coin and then a whisker's width from the other, and sends him both smells. His coin smells of him: leather, road sweat, the Saltwind's tar, and copper warmed by his own skin. It's familiar, a smell the cat would follow through any crowd. The other is copper warmed in a hand too, but not his hand and not Garret's either. Under it is the deep cold salt the cat has now found three times tonight. Of the two coins, only that one carries it. The cat pulls back from it and sits pressed against his shin.

Brask puts the lantern down. For a moment she looks at the door, then at the keeper, who hasn't moved. Then she takes the oilcloth book from inside her tabard again. This time she doesn't turn it away. She opens it to a page near the back, lays it flat on the slab beside the two coins, and puts her finger under the first line.

The handwriting is small, square and Fist-taught. There are seven names, each with a date, and next to each name a few words that have nothing to do with the sea.

*Wenna Tull, net-mender. Hauled up a purse in her net, 12 gp.*
*Orrin Vasse, carter. Dray overturned on Stonyhill, walked out from under it.*
*Halder Cobb, dicer. Won big, guest table.* In the margin, underlined twice: *the Wheel.*
*Tam Rook, deckhand. Aunt in Scornubel died, left him a house.*
*Sefton Marr, clerk. Debts paid off in one night.* In the margin: *the Wheel.*
*Nell, no other name. Survived the fever ward at Twin Songs.*
*Garret Hobb, porter. Three hands running at Malloway's crate.*

Every one of them was pulled out of the harbour, and every one had a copper in the mouth.

"Seven since the thaw," Brask says. "Filed as sea business, all seven. I asked one of Umberlee's women about the coins. She spat on the floor of the Fist hall, and I had to mop it." It comes out as flat as everything else she says. "You said receipt. You're the first person besides me to say it out loud."

She leaves the book open on the slab, but her hand stays flat beside it.

"The Wheel's a gaming house behind the inner wall. Patriar money, invitation only. The Watch's ground, not ours. I can't walk in there in this tabard." Her eyes go to his coin, then to his face. "So it's my turn, Worgen. Every name on that page had a stroke of luck in the month before the water took them."

She looks at him the same way she looked at him over the lantern on the quay.

"You crossed the sea to the Gate on the Lady's errand. Have you been lucky lately?"

turns.message:
I pick my coin up off the slab and settle the cord back around my neck. It's warm against my chest again. I take my time answering, because she asked a straight question and lying to her would be a poor way to start.

"Yes," I say. "The luckiest night of my life. A month and a bit ago, in a card room in the south, I put everything I owned on one hand. I was losing. I prayed to the Lady and the hand came good." I tap the coin. "She named her price, and I gave up cards for it. That's why I'm here." I look down at her list and the two words underlined in the margin. "So by your book, Sergeant, I'm about due for the harbour."

I don't make a joke of it. It comes out as flat as she talks. A soldier who's been told where the next arrow is likely to land doesn't make jokes about it.

"Here's what I see. Every one of them got lucky, and somebody took it back with interest. A man who won big at a guest table in the Wheel. A man whose debts vanished in one night. That isn't the sea collecting, it's a house collecting." I nod at the copper with the turned head. "And she's looking back at whoever's behind her, keeping the tally."

Then I meet Brask's eyes.

"You can't walk into the Wheel in that tabard. I'm a stranger with patriar-sized gold in my purse and a face I can change when I need to. I'd rather go looking for whoever's coming for me than wait for him on a dark quay." I keep my hands off her book. "Before I do, tell me one more thing. The two from the Wheel, Cobb and Marr: did anyone ever say who invited them in?"

Through the link, to the cat: *That smell is following people who've had luck. Which makes it ours now too. Stay close.*
turns.reply:
James lifts his coin off the slab and puts the cord back over his head. Brask doesn't stop him. She watches him take his time, and when he says *a month and a bit ago*, her pencil is already moving.

She doesn't interrupt. When he gets to *about due for the harbour*, she turns the oilcloth book back toward herself, finds the first blank line under Garret Hobb, and writes. She doesn't hide it this time. Upside down, in the same small square hand, he can read: *J. Worgen, sellsword, Tethyr. Won a hand in the south. Off the Saltwind, day of arrival.*

"So I know where to start," she says, "if it's you."

She lets *a house collecting* go by without a word, but she looks at the turned head on the copper again when he says it. When he offers to go where her tabard can't, she gives a short breath through her nose and says nothing at all for a moment. On his stool the keeper shifts and goes on snoring.

"Nobody said who invited them," she says at last. "I asked. Not in the Upper City. The Watch doesn't answer Fist questions, and my captain doesn't let me ask them." She taps Cobb's name with the end of her pencil. "Cobb bragged in a dice cellar on Tallow Lane. Said he'd had a hot night and a gentleman left something on his table and walked off. Said gentleman. Nothing more. He drowned eleven days later."

She goes to the shelf, runs a finger along the chalked lids and takes down a second box. *S. MARR.* It's lighter than Garret's. She sets it on the slab and lifts the lid.

There's a clerk's ink-stained cuff, an empty purse, and a pair of spectacles with one lens cracked. Wrapped in a twist of paper is a brass disc about the size of a gold piece. It's stamped on one face with an eight-spoked wheel, worn bright at the rim where a thumb has turned it over and over. The other face is plain except for a number scratched into it by hand: *7*.

"In his coat when they pulled him out. His sister took his clothes and left that. Said she didn't want it in the house." Brask doesn't touch it either. "I'd wager it's what gets a man through their door. I can't prove it."

Down by James's boot, the cat stretches its neck toward the slab, and the smell comes through the link before it pulls back. The brass smells of Marr's thumb, ink and old sweat. Over that is something that doesn't belong in a clerk's coat: wax, and a thick, sweet smoke like a censer, as if the disc had sat for a long time in a room where something was burned for someone. Very faint, underneath all of it, is the cold deep salt again. The cat doesn't back away this time. It presses against James's shin and stays there, and its tail wraps around his ankle.

Brask folds her arms.

"It's Fist property. If I lend it out, it goes in my book with your name and the hour, same as you did." Her eyes stay on his face. "And if a dead man's marker turns up at their door in a stranger's hand, someone there will know whose it was. They'll know it before you've sat down."

She leaves the disc lying in its paper between them and doesn't push it toward him.

"So tell me how you'd use it, Worgen. Not that you'd go. How."

turns.message:
I look at the brass wheel for a while without reaching for it. The scratched *7* bothers me more than the spokes.

"Not at their door," I say. "You're right. If they number them, they know whose seven that is, and a dead clerk's marker in a stranger's hand is a confession before I've opened my mouth. Whoever holds it walks into a room where they've already decided the ending."

I straighten up and count it off on my fingers, the way we planned a scout back in Tethyr.

"First, I don't go to the Wheel. The Wheel comes to me. By your book I'm already the kind of man they collect: off a boat, a winner, the Lady's coin on my chest. Cobb said a *gentleman* left something on his table. So I go where Cobb went, the dice cellar on Tallow Lane, and I let the right sort of people see I'm flush and favoured. I don't play. I watch who's watching. If somebody leaves a brass wheel on my table, I'll know the hand that put it there, and that tells us more than a dead man's marker ever will."

Second finger.

"Second, the marker stays dark. I carry it sewn into my cloak and nobody sees it. It's only there in case I need to prove something, or to set it beside whatever they hand me and see whether the numbers run in order. If they're counting, I want to know where the count stands."

Third.

"Third, if I ever do show it, it won't be on this face." I touch my cheek. "I can wear another man's, for an hour or a night. Not Marr's, they'd know a ghost. But a stranger who found it in a dead man's coat and wants to sell it back. That's a different conversation, and an honest one, in its way. Whoever comes to buy it is your man, or works for him."

I let my hand drop.

"And you get everything, Sergeant. Where I go, who I talk to, when I come back. If I miss a meeting, you'll know which page to start on." I nod at her book. "Write it down. My name, the hour, *borrowed for the Wheel*. Where do I find you tomorrow, if not at a dead-house?"

Through the link, to the cat: *Smoke, wax, a burning room. If you smell that anywhere in this city, wake me. Even in my sleep.*
turns.reply:
Brask hears him out with her arms folded. She doesn't interrupt and she doesn't nod. When he gets to *the Wheel comes to me*, her eyes go to the box, and they stay there through the second finger and the third. When he touches his cheek, she looks up at his face as if she's trying to work out how much of it is his.

When his hand drops, she waits a moment longer to make sure he's done.

"One thing's wrong with it." She taps the edge of the slab beside the paper twist. "You don't sell it back. It's Fist property and evidence. You can show it, wave it, let a man see the seven. If it leaves your hand, I've lost the only thing on this shelf that came from inside that house." A pause. "Nobody buys back something worthless. Let them think you'll sell. Then don't."

She unfolds her arms, picks up the paper by its corners and wraps the brass disc again, one fold and then another, so the wheel and the seven both disappear. She doesn't hand it to him yet. First the oilcloth book comes out, open to the page with his name on it, and she writes under that line without hiding it:

*Lent: brass marker, S. Marr, wheel and 7. To J. Worgen. 20th hour, day of arrival. Tallow Lane, not the door.*

She turns the book so he can read it, then shuts it.

"Tallow Lane. Cobb's cellar is under the chandler's with the drowned-candle sign, three doors up from the tannery. They call it Kettle's. It's Guild ground. The Guild won't care what you watch so long as you don't win in there. If you don't play, they'll wonder why you came. Have an answer ready."

She holds the paper twist out across the slab at arm's length, the way she handed back his pay slip.

"The checkpoint, from midday until the lamps. Before midday, leave word with him." She tips her chin at the old keeper, who hasn't moved since they came in. "He can't read, so he won't."

When James takes the marker, it's lighter than he expected, and colder. The cat stretches up against his shin to get its nose near the paper. Through the link comes the same smell as before, wax and that thick sweet smoke, now so close it seems to coat the back of his throat. The answer to his order comes after it. It isn't a word. It's the feeling of the cat settling in for a long watch, the way it settles on a sill at dusk: ears turned outward, the whole city sorted into what it has already smelled and what it hasn't yet. *Even in your sleep.* The tail stays wrapped around his ankle.

Brask puts Marr's box back on the shelf, then Garret's beside it, chalked names facing out. She lifts her lantern.

"Kettle's stays busy until the bells at two. Tansy Brindle's door shuts at midnight, if that's where the lad sent you." She doesn't ask whether it was. "I'll walk out with you as far as the causeway. After that the quay's yours."

At the door she stops with her hand on the latch and looks back once at the shelf of pine boxes.

"Eight lines, Worgen. I'd rather not write a ninth." She opens the door onto the cold and the slap of the harbour. "Next."

turns.message:
I tuck the paper twist inside my shirt, under the coin, where I'll feel it if anyone's fingers go looking. Then I walk out beside her lantern as far as the causeway, on her lantern side, keeping the same arm's length.

At the causeway I stop.

"I'll answer Kettle's question tomorrow night, not tonight. I want to see the room before it sees me, and I'd rather not walk into Guild ground with a pack on my back and nothing but gold in my purse." I touch two fingers to my brow, the old Tethyrian salute, lazy from years out of the ranks. "Midday at the checkpoint, Sergeant. If I'm not there, start on page eight."

Then I go back along the quay and turn up Cable Lane, where the lamps are lit, the way Pip told me. I keep to the middle of the lane, away from doorways. The Boots let me walk quietly, but I don't hurry. A man who hurries looks like he has something worth following.

Through the link, to the cat: *Behind us again, ten paces. Anything that smells of deep salt or that smoke, stop and look at me.*

At the narrow house with the blue door behind the ropewalk, I knock and wait where the landlady can see my hands.

"Evening. Pip Malloway sent me, so I expect it's six silver." I hold up a single gold piece. "A room for a few nights, if you've got one, and change for this, as much as you'll give. And a needle and thread, if you can spare them. I've got a cloak lining to mend."
turns.reply:
James tucks the paper twist inside his shirt, under the cord, where the brass lies cold against his skin. He walks out beside Brask on her lantern side, keeping the same arm's length, and the dead-house door bangs shut behind them in the wind off the water.

At the causeway she stops when he does. She listens to the part about tomorrow night without interrupting, and when his two fingers come up to his brow, her eyes follow them. Her face doesn't change. Her own hand moves a little at her side, the start of a Fist salute that she doesn't finish.

"Line eight," she says. "It's all one page."

Then she turns onto the causeway toward the Seatower, and the lantern gets smaller over the black water until the gate swallows it.

The quay is quieter on the way back. Past the checkpoint, the young relief soldier sits hunched over the ledger with his tabard bunched up at the shoulders, and he doesn't look up. Pip's crate stands empty at the edge of the stones. The cards are gone, and a single copper lies forgotten in a crack beside it. Across the way, the salt-house doorway is only a doorway.

The cat drops back its ten paces as soon as James turns uphill. Through the link comes Cable Lane at a foot off the ground. Hemp dust drifts from the ropewalk, long and dry. Fish-heads lie in a gutter, and a dog has left its mark on every second post. Behind a shutter someone is frying onions in old fat. A child is crying two houses over and then stops. The cat pauses at every doorway he passes and sorts it, smelled or not yet smelled. There's no deep salt in any of them, and no smoke or wax. Once it stops dead at the mouth of an alley and James feels its whole body go tight. Then it's a rat, and the cat lets it go, which it would never do on an ordinary night.

Nobody follows them. The lamps run all the way up.

The blue door is narrower than the houses on either side, as though someone fitted it into a gap that was never meant to hold a house. James knocks and steps back where the lamp falls on his hands. A small shutter at halfling height slides open. An eye looks at his hands, then his face, then down at the cat sitting on the step, then up at his face again.

When he says *Pip Malloway*, the eye narrows.

The door opens on a chain. Tansy Brindle is perhaps three feet of grey-haired halfling in a flour-dusted apron, with a candle in one hand and an iron poker in the other. She doesn't seem to think the poker needs explaining.

"Six," she agrees, and holds out the candle hand for the coin. "He sends me a soldier with gold. Last month he sent me a juggler with fleas." She bites the gold piece hard, frowns at it, then frowns at him. "Gold. As if I keep a counting-house in my apron." She goes off muttering, and James hears a box rattle somewhere inside. She comes back with four silver pieces and counts them into his palm one at a time, hard, like a grudge. "There. And don't you dare give me another one of those tomorrow. You pay each morning, before porridge. I don't keep accounts, I keep lodgers who are alive at breakfast."

The chain comes off. Inside, the house smells of tallow, bread and lavender stuffed into a mattress somewhere. The stairs are steep and so narrow that his pack scrapes both walls.

"Top room. Window over the ropewalk. If you hear singing at two in the morning, that's the Lantzers next door and not a ghost. Door's bolted at midnight. After that I don't open it for the Fist, the Guild or the Grand Dukes in their nightshirts." She digs in her apron pocket and slaps a needle, stuck through a fold of card with brown thread wound round it, onto the newel post. "Lent, not given. I count my needles."

The cat steps over the threshold as if it owned the place. Tansy looks down at it and the poker comes up an inch.

"And that one. Is it yours, or did it just come in?"

turns.message:
"Mine," I say, and crouch so the cat and I are at her height. "Or I'm his. We haven't settled which. He's tidier than I am, and he catches anything with more legs than he's got. If he so much as looks at your larder, put it on my porridge bill."

I pick the needle off the newel post and hold it up so she can see where it's going. "Back on this post before breakfast. Counted."

Then I squeeze up the stairs with the pack scraping both walls. Once the door's shut behind me, I go to the window and check it: the latch, the drop to the ropewalk, whether there's a ledge a man could stand on. I leave the shutter open a crack.

I unpick a hand's width of the cloak's hem lining on the inside, low at the back near the regimental patch where the wool is doubled. I slide the paper twist with Marr's marker in, flat, and stitch it shut with small soldier's stitches, the kind we used for coins on campaign. Then I test it with my fingers until I can feel the disc but can't see it.

Through the link, to the cat: *Take the windowsill. Watch the lane and the ropewalk till the bells. Wake me for salt, smoke, wax, or anyone who stops under this window twice.*

Then I lay the deck of cards on the table, still in its case, where I'll see it first thing, take off my boots, keep the rapier within reach of the bed, and sleep.
turns.reply:
James crouches until he and the cat are both at Tansy's height. She listens to *or I'm his* with her mouth pressed flat, and when he gets to the porridge bill she gives a short sound through her nose. It could have been a laugh.

"Porridge bill." She looks the cat up and down while it sits on her doormat and washes one paw as if the house had been built around it. "There's a tom two doors down with half an ear who thinks this lane belongs to him. You tell yours the larder's mine and the yard's his business." She watches the needle go up between James's fingers. "Counted," she agrees, flat as Brask. "Porridge at first light. Silver first."

The stairs are as narrow going up as they looked from below. The pack scrapes plaster on both sides the whole way. The top room is under the roof, low enough that James has to duck at the edges. It holds a bed with a lavender-stuffed mattress, a three-legged table, a washbasin with a crack mended in pitch, and a hook on the door.

He checks the window first. The latch is a plain iron hook in a frame swollen with damp, so the shutter sticks and has to be lifted to open. There's no ledge outside, just a lip of crumbling mortar two fingers wide that wouldn't hold a pigeon. About twelve feet down, the long tarred roof of the ropewalk runs off into the dark, with hemp dust lying on it like frost. A man couldn't stand outside this window. A man with a short ladder on that roof could reach it, though, and a man going out this way could drop onto that roof and come up limping. James notes both and leaves the shutter open a crack.

He sits on the bed with the cloak across his knees. The regimental patch at the back is where the wool is doubled, the same as every Zaranda cloak he ever wore. Unpicking a hand's width of the lining takes a few minutes with the point of Tansy's needle. The paper twist slides in flat and cold. He closes the gap with small, tight stitches, the kind men on campaign used to keep their pay out of the dice games and away from the sergeants, and ties off the brown thread in a knot nobody will notice. Then he runs his fingers along the hem twice. He can feel the disc, but he can't see it, not even holding the cloth up to the candle.

The cat jumps to the sill when he tells it to, turns around once, and settles with its tail hanging over the edge. Through the link comes the lane below at a cat's angle: the lamp at the corner, the wet cobbles, the ropewalk roof grey with dust. Its attention narrows and stays fixed there, like a door being held open.

The deck goes on the table in its worn case, where the first light will fall on it. Boots off. The rapier goes against the bedframe where his hand can find it. The candle goes out.

---

The night passes, and the cat watches all of it.

James doesn't wake, but the link keeps carrying things into his sleep the way a river carries sticks. Somewhere toward the middle of the night a Fist patrol goes by with two lanterns, and boots ring and fade. A drunk stops under the corner lamp to argue with it and moves on. The half-eared tom from two doors down comes along the ropewalk roof, finds a cat in the window, and the two of them stare at each other for a long, silent time until the tom decides he had somewhere else to be. At the second bell the Lantzers next door start singing. It's something about a sailor and a widow in Amn, in three voices, two of them flat, and it goes on for six verses.

No one stops under the window twice. There's no deep salt in the air except the ordinary harbour kind, and no smoke or wax anywhere. The cat never wakes him.

---

Grey light comes through the crack in the shutter and falls across the table, the way he meant it to. The first thing James sees when he opens his eyes is the card case: the worn corners, the stain on the lid from a tavern in Myratma, the flap still shut.

The cat is still on the sill. It hasn't moved since he lay down, apart from its tail. When it feels him wake, it sends him the night all at once and with no order to it: patrol, drunk, tom, singing, nothing. Under all of it comes something that isn't a picture. It's the stiffness of a long watch kept, and a clear expectation that something is owed for it.

Somewhere below, a pot lid clangs. Tansy's voice comes up the stairwell, sharp enough to carry through three floors of plaster.

"First light, soldier. Silver on the table before a spoon touches a bowl. And my needle."

 *Out of game:* none of these four needed a roll, and the narration already shows each one done:

1. **Sewing the marker into the hem:** he did it alone in a locked room, with no time pressure and nobody watching, so it couldn't go wrong. If someone searches the cloak later, their search roll will be tested against this hiding place then.
2. **Checking the window:** he looked at the latch, the drop and the ledge in his own room with a candle, at no risk. You got the full answer: an iron hook latch, no ledge, and the ropewalk roof about 12 feet below.
3. **The cat's night watch:** the cat stood watch, but nothing tried to slip past it, so there was nothing to roll its Perception against. The night was quiet, and the cat never woke him.
4. **The deck on the table:** putting a card case down has no uncertainty. It's lying there in the morning light.

turns.message:
I sit up and look at the card case for a moment. I don't open it. I tuck it into the bottom of my pack, under the bedroll, where my hand would have to go looking for it.

Then the cat. It earned its keep, and a soldier pays the sentry first. *Good watch. Breakfast's on me, the best of whatever's in my bowl.* I scratch it behind the ears the way it allows on its better days.

Boots on, cloak on. I run my fingers along the hem once to feel the disc, and go down the narrow stairs with the needle held up in front of me like a candle.

"Your needle, Mistress Brindle. Counted, and short only the thread." I put it on the newel post where she left it. Then I set a single gold piece on the table, flat, and keep my finger on it before she can start in. "No change. That's tonight, and the rest is credit against tomorrow. Saves us both the grudge."

While she decides whether that insults her, I sit down to the porridge and keep my voice easy.

"Two things a stranger can't ask in the street. Where does an honest man change gold in the Lower City without the Guild hearing about it by noon? And the Ammersteads, the salt family up the hill. What does the lane say about them?"

I set half my bowl's milk down on the floor for the cat, and wait for her answer.
turns.reply:
The card case goes into the bottom of the pack, under the bedroll. To get at it now, a hand would have to go digging.

The cat takes the scratch behind the ears with its eyes half shut, as if it were rent it had been owed all night. When James sends it the promise about breakfast, it gets down off the sill, stretches each back leg separately, and goes down the stairs ahead of him with its tail straight up.

Cloak on. His fingers run along the hem and find the disc, flat and cold where he left it. The needle goes down the narrow stairs ahead of him, held up like a candle.

The kitchen is the whole back of the house: a hearth, a scrubbed table, and a window onto a yard the width of a door. Tansy is at the pot with a ladle as long as her arm. She watches the needle go onto the newel post and counts it with a glance, one needle, then turns back to the pot. When the gold piece goes down on the table under his finger, she puts the ladle down.

She waits until he has finished. Then she walks over, gets two fingers under the edge of the coin and slides it back across the table until it bumps his hand.

"I don't keep accounts," she says. "I said it at the door and I'll say it at my own table. Credit's how the Lantzers ended up owing me for a whole winter, and singing about it." She looks at the coin and then at him. "You've got four of my silver in your purse from last night. Put those down and you owe me two by lamplighting. I'll remember them, which isn't the same as keeping accounts."

All the same, she puts a bowl of porridge in front of him, thick and grey, with a skin of milk on top and salt in it the Gate way. When he tips half his milk onto the floor, she watches it run toward the hearthstones and says nothing. The cat starts on it as if the house had been built for that purpose.

She takes up the ladle again and answers him with her back half turned. It's the way people here talk when they don't want it to count as gossip.

"Changing gold. The Guild hears it by noon wherever you do it, so don't pay extra for wishing. The Counting House changes it fair. They take a copper on the piece and write your name in a big book, and they don't sell the book. A moneychanger in the market takes a tenth and talks for free." A sniff. "Pick which you'd rather have, your name written down or your business told."

The ladle scrapes the bottom of the pot.

"The Ammersteads. My mother remembered old Ammerstead's father carrying salt on his own back on that quay, in a sack, like a porter. His son had a counting-room. *His* son was made a patriar, and now there's a salt-cellar on a coat of arms that nobody's allowed to laugh at." She taps the ladle on the rim. "That's two lifetimes. It took the Lantzers two lifetimes to buy a second chair. The lane says the Ammersteads have never lost a ship, not one in sixty years. The Fishers lost three this spring, and the Fishers have prayed to Umberlee since before the wall." Another sniff. "People say it's good management, the way they'd say a dog's friendly while it's still showing its teeth."

She puts the ladle down and wipes her hands on the apron. Flour comes off in a cloud.

"And there's this, since you're asking things a stranger can't ask in the street. This past month there've been men in good boots out past the wall, Rivington way, asking after a young gentleman. They pay for answers and they pay well. The lane says it's an Ammerstead pup who's run off." She looks at him straight. "Men in boots like that don't come asking down Cable Lane, and I'd like to keep it that way."

The cat finishes the milk and sits down to wash. Tansy holds out her hand, palm up, flour in the creases, waiting for the four silver.

turns.message:
I count the four silver into her floury palm one at a time, slowly and with feeling, the way she counted them into mine.

"One. Two. Three. Four. And two more by lamplighting, remembered, not accounted." I finish the porridge. It's better than anything the Saltwind's cook managed in three weeks, and I tell her so. "Sixty years without losing a ship, while the Fishers pray and drown. I'll keep that in mind, Mistress. And men in good boots stay off Cable Lane. If they come asking, I was never here and the cat's yours."

I stand, settle the cloak, and feel the hem once more out of habit.

Then out into the morning, uphill toward the Counting House. I'd rather have my name in a book that isn't sold than my business told at a market stall, and Brask already has my name in hers. I'll change about fifty gold into silver and copper. A man going to Kettle's tonight should have small coin to spend on drink, not gold that makes the Guild sit up.

Through the link, to the cat: *Ten paces back again. Deep salt, that smoke, good boots, or the same face twice, tell me.*

On the way I keep my eyes open for a cloth-seller or a secondhand stall. I want something a little better than road leather for tonight, a coat a flush stranger would wear, so the room sees money before it sees a soldier.
turns.reply:
James counts the silver into Tansy's palm one coin at a time, pressing each one down hard enough to leave a mark in the flour. She watches every coin land. Her mouth stays flat until the fourth, and then one corner of it gives a little.

"Remembered," she says. "Not accounted." Her fist closes over the four.

When he tells her the porridge beat three weeks of ship's cooking, she sniffs as if he'd said the sea was wet. "Ship's cooks boil oats in bilge and blame the weather." That's the closest she comes to taking the compliment. She takes the empty bowl out from under his spoon before he's quite done with it.

At *the cat's yours* she looks down at the animal, which is washing behind one ear on her hearthstone.

"I don't want your cat. If anyone asks, I'll say it came in on its own, and that's no lie, is it?" She turns back to the pot. "Off with you. Lamplighting. Two."

---

Cable Lane is a different street by daylight. The ropewalk doors stand open, and inside men walk backward down the long shed, paying out hemp from their waists. Dust hangs in the sunlight like flour. Further up, the tannery's smell rolls downhill to meet them. Fishwives on the corner are already arguing over the night's catch.

The cat drops back its ten paces as soon as they're out the door. Through the link the morning arrives in pieces: hot bread from a bakehouse grate, wet tar, a dog that wants to make friends and gets ignored, and the tannery, which is so strong the cat sneezes twice and shuts it out. There's no deep salt in any of it, and no smoke or wax. No face turns up twice.

Halfway up, where Cable Lane meets a wider street climbing toward the market, a row of old-clothes stalls is just setting up under the eaves of a shuttered chapel. One rail catches James's eye as he passes. The woman hanging it is a tiefling, tall and spare, with the tips of her horns filed blunt and a mouthful of pins. Among the shirts she's putting out is a coat cut long in the southern way, in bottle-green wool, with a velvet collar worn shiny at the nape. It's the kind of coat a merchant captain buys when his first good voyage pays out. She sees him look. She doesn't call out. She just turns the coat a little on its hook so the light falls on the buttons.

He keeps walking.

The Counting House sits at the top of the market slope. It's square, grey, and built to look as if it has never once been robbed. The doors open at the seventh bell, and James is fifth in line. The ones ahead of him are a chandler with a strongbox, a widow with a letter of credit, and two sailors pooling their pay.

On the steps, the cat stops dead.

Through the link comes a picture from a foot off the ground: two pairs of boots on either side of the doorway pillar. They're oiled calfskin, blacked that morning, and the welts are clean. There's no salt crust, and no street muck above the sole. The cat sends the smell with them: horse, good soap, and the bitter wax of boot-blacking. These are boots for riding and standing in, not for walking the Lower City.

James lets his eyes rise above the boots without lifting his head. Two men in plain brown cloaks, one leaning on the pillar with a copy of *Baldur's Mouth* folded open. He isn't reading it. Everyone who goes in through the door gets a look from both of them: first the face, then a quick reckoning of age, and then they look away. When James's turn comes, their eyes stay on him for about as long as it takes to see a man of thirty-odd with a soldier's cloak and road on his face. Then they let him go. Whoever they want, it isn't him.

Inside, the hall is cool and echoes, and it smells of ink and brass polish. The ledger James was promised really is a big one. It sits open on a lectern behind the counter, chained to it at the spine. The clerk who serves him is a gnome perched on a tall stool, with spectacles pushed up onto a bald head and a second pair on his nose. He hears *fifty gold into silver and copper* without looking up.

"A copper a piece for the changing. That's fifty copper, out of the copper." He dips his quill. "Name, for the book."

James gives it. The quill scratches. Upside down, James reads: *J. Worgen. 50 gp to small coin. 7th bell.* The gnome weighs the gold on a brass scale, then counts silver out in stacks of ten: forty-five stacks. After that come the coppers, poured into a pan and weighed, not counted: five hundred, less his fifty. He sweeps it all into two canvas bags and ties them off.

"Four hundred fifty silver, four hundred fifty copper." He finally looks up, over both pairs of spectacles, at the bags and then at James. "That's near eighteen pounds of coin, sir. Folk usually ask for less of it." He goes back to his ledger. "Next."

The bags go into the bottom of the pack, next to the card case, and the pack sits heavier on James's shoulders than it did on the Saltwind's gangplank. When he comes out, the two men in good boots are still at the pillar. One has turned a page of the broadsheet he isn't reading.

Halfway back down the slope, the old-clothes row is properly open now. The tiefling has finished with her pins. She leans on the post of her rail with her arms folded, and the bottle-green coat hangs at the end where anyone coming downhill can see it.

"You looked at it on the way up," she says as he gets near. Her voice is dry and low, with a lilt from somewhere upriver. "That's a Calishite cut. It came off a captain who doesn't need it now. One button's horn, the rest are brass, and the sleeves run half an inch short on a man your size." She takes it off the hook and holds it up by the shoulders, so the velvet collar catches the light. "Four gold, and I'll sew on a brass button to match before you walk off. Three if you pay in silver and don't make me count it."

turns.message:
I stop at her rail and take the coat by the sleeve, not the collar. I turn the cuff back to look at the lining, the stitching and the wear at the elbows, the way you'd check a horse's teeth.

"Three, in silver, and you won't need to count it, because I will." I set the pack down, dig out one of the canvas bags, and stack thirty silver on the board of her stall in three neat towers of ten. "And the brass button. A man should match himself."

While she threads her needle, I slip the coat on over the leather. The sleeves are short, just as she said. I shrug the soldier's cloak back on over it so the patch still sits where it should.

"A captain who doesn't need it now," I say lightly, looking down the slope rather than at her. "Gone home to Calimshan, or gone into the harbour?" I let that sit a moment. "I ask because I've just come from a place where they keep men's boots in boxes, and nobody on this quay seems to die of old age."

Then, quieter, with a nod uphill toward the Counting House: "Two fellows in good boots up there are reading the same page of *Baldur's Mouth* all morning and looking at every young face that goes through the door. You've got a rail on the main slope, Mistress. Seen them before?"

Through the link, to the cat: *Smell the coat when I'm done. Tell me if it's been near the water, or that smoke.*
turns.reply:
James takes the coat by the sleeve, not the collar, and turns the cuff back. Patience watches him do it without comment. The lining is green silk gone brown at the seams. The stitching is small and even, sailmaker's work rather than a tailor's, and it has been redone once at the left shoulder. The elbows are worn shiny but not thin. Somebody looked after this coat.

When the canvas bag comes out of the pack and the silver goes down on her board in three towers of ten, she doesn't count it. She stoops a little and squints along the tops of the stacks to check they stand level. Then she sweeps all three into her palm in one movement and drops them into a tin under the rail.

"Your counting is good enough for me," she says, around the pins.

The coat goes on over his leather. The sleeves stop half an inch short of his wrists, just as she said. With the soldier's cloak back over his shoulders and the patch where it belongs, he looks like what he has been trying to look like: a man whose last voyage paid out, with money to spend.

Patience takes a pin from her mouth and threads a needle without looking at it. "Hold still. I don't take a coat back off a man once he's paid for it." She snips the horn button free at his breast and drops it into the tin with the silver. She takes a brass one from a twist of paper, sets it in the gap and starts stitching. Her head is level with his collarbone and her filed horns are an inch from his chin. Her hands are quick and cool.

When he asks about the captain, the needle doesn't stop.

"It came to me dry," she says. The thread goes through and pulls tight. "Out of a sea chest, folded, with camphor in the pockets. Whatever happened to the man, it didn't happen in this coat." She leaves it there. She doesn't say whose chest it was.

Down at his boot, the cat has already put its nose to the hem. Through the link it sends what it finds: cedarwood, and the bitter camphor she mentioned. There's old pipe tobacco worked into the wool. It's sweet and brown, and the cat sorts it straight away as nothing like the thick censer smoke on Marr's marker. Hair oil at the velvet collar comes from a man who isn't here. Over all of it lies the warm, dry smell of Patience's own hands. The cat finds no harbour water and no deep salt. Nothing about the coat has been near the sea except the man who owned it. The cat sneezes once at the camphor and sits down, satisfied.

At *two fellows in good boots*, Patience's eyes go up the slope toward the Counting House. They come back to the button.

"Yesterday, and the day before." She wraps the thread three times under the button to make a shank. "They came down the row asking trader's questions. Had anybody sold us good clothes lately? Fine linen, a young gentleman's coat, maybe a ring. Soft hands, fair hair, about twenty." She bites the thread off. "They paid a silver at every rail just for asking. Generous."

She smooths the cloth flat around the new button with her thumb and steps back to look at it.

"I didn't have what they were looking for."

She says it the way she said *it came to me dry*, carefully, every word picked. It's the kind of answer a trader gives when someone else's question is too wide for her to want to answer it as asked. *Didn't have* isn't the same as *never saw*.

She puts the needle back in its card and looks past him down the slope, toward the street that leads to the quay.

"The Fist comes round this row at the eighth bell and moves on anyone with horns." It isn't a complaint, just the time of day. "It suits you better than it suited him. Is there anything else, soldier?"

turns.message:
I run my thumb over the new button. It sits flat and true, and it matches.

"Good work. Better than the man who sewed the shoulder." I pick up the pack and settle it, then speak quietly, looking at her rail instead of at her, the way she's been doing with me.

"I'm not with the boots, Mistress, and I'm not in the business of selling young men back to their fathers. Whatever you didn't have is your affair." I put one more silver on her board, next to the tin. "That's for the horn button. I'd like it back someday, if I come asking."

Then, more quietly still: "If a lad with soft hands ever needs a coat that doesn't look like a gentleman's, or a bed behind a door that won't open for the Fist or the Guild, there's a blue door on Cable Lane behind the ropewalk. Tansy Brindle. She's sharp, she counts her needles, and she doesn't ask names." I touch two fingers to my brow. "James Worgen, if anyone wants to know who sent him. What do I call you?"

Whatever she answers, I don't linger. The eighth bell is coming, and I don't want her seen talking to a stranger when the Fist walks the row.

Through the link, to the cat: *Remember her smell. Hands, pins, camphor. She's a friend until she shows us otherwise.*

Then downhill toward the tannery. I want to find the chandler's with the drowned-candle sign on Tallow Lane by daylight: which door, which way the cellar steps face, where a man could stand across the street, and how many ways out there are. I'll walk past once without stopping, then head down to the checkpoint for midday.
turns.reply:
James runs his thumb over the new button. It sits flat and true, and it matches the others.

When he praises her stitching over the shoulder repair, Patience looks at the shoulder, not at him. Something in her face suggests she noticed that seam herself some time ago and decided not to mention it.

She doesn't answer *I'm not with the boots.* She takes a pin out of her mouth, then another, and pushes them into the cushion on her wrist. When the extra silver goes down on her board beside the tin, she looks at it for a moment without picking it up.

"A silver for a horn button," she says. "That's a poor price, Master Worgen, for you." Her long fingers go into the tin anyway. She doesn't take the silver out. She takes the horn button, turns it once in the light, and drops it into the pocket of her apron, apart from the stock. Then the silver goes into the tin.

At *Cable Lane* she goes still for a moment, the way a trader does when she's working out a figure. "Cable Lane. Behind the ropewalk. Blue door." She says it under her breath, like someone fixing a price in her head, and doesn't ask any questions. "I sell coats. I don't keep a list of doors."

That doesn't mean she'll forget it.

When his two fingers come up to his brow, she answers with her name and nothing else.

"Patience Vell."

Then she turns the next coat on its hook toward the light, and he's a customer who has finished his business.

The cat has been sitting at the corner of her rail. It stretches its neck toward the hem of her skirt, and James gets what it took: cool, dry hands; steel pins; camphor; and under those, very faint, old smoke. It isn't censer smoke. It's the smoke of wood and pitch burned a long time ago, the kind that never really leaves a refugee's clothes. The cat files her away somewhere between *smelled* and *safe*, then falls in ten paces behind him.

Halfway down the slope, two Fist soldiers in red tabards come up past him with a handcart and the bored walk of men doing the same round they did yesterday. Neither of them looks at a man in a merchant's green coat. Behind him, he hears the rails on the row start to rattle.

---

Tallow Lane is easy to find. You follow your nose. The tannery stands at the bottom of it, a long brick shed with vats steaming in the yard, and the stink of lime and bark rolls up the lane so thick the cat sneezes and shuts it out of the link. Three doors up is a chandler's with a painted sign: a blue candle standing upside down in painted water, wick first, its flame still burning under the waves.

James doesn't slow down. Up close, a man of Zaranda's scouts doesn't look at a target. He looks at the street around it.

He gets the obvious parts. Kettle's has a single outside stair. It drops down beside the chandler's door to a squat oak door with iron straps, chained shut for the daylight hours. The steps face uphill, so anyone coming down them has the lane at his back. Across the street a cooper's yard has barrels stacked head-high against the wall, and a man could stand in their shadow half the night and look like he was waiting for a barrel. Further up, a laundry spills steam from its windows. Below it all, the tannery yard is open to the lane, with vats, carts and a gate that never seems to shut.

But one pass doesn't tell him more than that. He can't see a back way, though a dice cellar the Guild has run for years must have one. If the Guild keeps eyes on this lane by day, they're better hidden than he is from his angle, or he walked straight past them. All he sees is ordinary morning: a chandler's girl sweeping the step, a carter cursing a mule, a boy on the cooper's mounting block whittling a stick. When James looks back from the corner, the boy is gone from the block. That could mean anything, or nothing.

The cat comes past the cellar stair ten paces behind him. It doesn't stop, but its nose drags along the bottom of the iron handrail for a stride. Through the link James gets tallow, spilled ale, a hundred hands on the rail, vomit somebody washed off yesterday and didn't wash off well. Under all of that, faint and a day or two old, he gets wet wool that has dried and got wet again, lamp-black, and the cold, clean salt of deep water.

The grey man has been down these steps.

The cat lifts its head and walks on without looking back, the way James taught it. Its tail is stiff all the way to the corner.

At the top of Tallow Lane the bells of the Lower City start the ninth hour, one after another and out of step, from towers he can't see yet.

---

*Out of game: it's about 9 in the morning. The checkpoint is a quarter-hour walk down to the quay, and Brask isn't there until midday, so you have roughly three hours. Do you go straight down and wait, or do something else first?*

 James's scout's eye let him down this morning. He went down Tallow Lane and back up it once, as planned, and came away with only what any carter could see. He didn't find a second door into Kettle's, didn't spot anyone keeping watch on it, and can't say who saw him studying the place. If he wants the back way and the Guild's lookouts, he'll have to get them some other way.

turns.message:
The grey man has been down those steps. I file it away for Brask and keep walking. I don't look back at the cooper's block. If the boy was a Guild lookout, he's seen a flush stranger in a green coat looking over a dice cellar, which is about what I want them to see before tonight.

Cable Lane is on my way to the quay, so I stop at the blue door first. Eighteen pounds of coin on my back and a crossbow on my pack don't fit the man I'm meant to be. Up in the top room I leave the bags under the mattress. I keep about forty silver and a fistful of copper in my purse, and the gold in the belt pouch against my skin. The crossbow goes behind the washbasin. I latch the shutter and wedge it with a fold of card. If I find it moved tonight, I'll know someone was here.

Then down to the quay. I don't go to the checkpoint yet. I want somewhere with a view of the salt-house where a man in a good coat can sit for an hour without being remarked on: a bench outside a waterfront alehouse, a coil of rope, a bollard in the sun. I pay a copper for a mug of small beer and put my back to a wall.

Through the link, to the cat: *The salt-house. In by the doorway or round by any gap you find, high or low. I'll be blind while you look, so be quick and don't let anyone see you. I want the inner door we heard shut, where it goes, and whether that deep salt is strongest there. If anything moves, come straight back to me.*

I close my eyes as if I'm dozing in the sun, keep one hand on my mug and the other near the rod under my coat, and go with it.
turns.reply:
James keeps walking and doesn't look back. A lookout, if that's what the boy was, has just watched a man in a green coat get interested in a dice cellar. The man in the green coat is happy to let him tell someone.

---

Tansy is on her knees scrubbing the front step when he comes back down Cable Lane. She looks at the pack, then at him, and sits back on her heels.

"Rent's lamplighting. Not breakfast, not dinner, lamplighting."

"I know. I'm leaving weight, not paying it."

She sniffs and goes back to the step. He squeezes past her and up the narrow stairs.

Up in the top room he works fast. The two canvas bags go under the mattress, one at the head end and one at the foot, so a hand sweeping under it won't find both at once. He counts forty silver and a fistful of copper into his purse. The gold goes into the flat pouch inside his shirt, against his skin, under the cord and the coin. He pushes the crossbow and its bolts behind the washbasin, where the pitch-mended crack throws a shadow. He lifts the swollen shutter onto its hook, folds a scrap of card twice and wedges it between the frame and the sill, low down where nobody would think to look for it. James keeps his hand on the cat's back. Under his palm the washing slows from frantic to merely thorough. When it stops to draw breath, he flicks two fingers at its face over the rim of the mug and murmurs the cantrip under the noise of the quay.

A small cool breath crosses the cat's muzzle. The salt crust lifts off its whiskers in a faint glitter and is gone, and its nose is clean and damp again. The cat sneezes once and holds very still, testing the air. Through the link James feels the quay come back to it one smell at a time: tar, fish, small beer, the cooper's shavings, his own boot. The deep salt is still lodged somewhere behind its eyes, but its nose works again. It gives his wrist one rough lick, the kind it saves for when it agrees with him, and settles against his boot with its back to the salt-house.

The beer goes down slowly, the way a man drinks when he has nowhere to be. Then he takes the empty mug back to the hatch himself and sets a second copper beside it.

The big woman looks at the copper before she looks at him. Up close her forearms are freckled to the elbow, and there's a burn scar across one thumb from a tap or a kettle.

He asks his questions lightly, a merchant thinking about rents. The coat says ship's money. The soldier's cloak over it says something else, and she's had both in front of her hatch all her life.

She weighs the copper, the coat and the cloak, and the coat wins. Her eyes go across the cobbles to the salt-house and come back with the look quay people give a newcomer who's about to throw money at the wrong thing.

"Ammersteads," she says. "Up the hill. You'd go knock at their gate and ask for their man of business, and he'd have you shown back down before you'd finished asking. That place isn't for rent and it isn't for sale. My da poured beer at this hatch, and it wasn't for sale in his day either." She wipes the mug with a rag that's seen better years. "Out of the Fist's eye is Guild business, master. You talk to them about landing things, not me. Mind you, even the Guild leaves that door alone. Make of that what you like."

She sets the mug upside down on the board, then leans on her forearms. Her voice drops. Something in her has wanted to say this to somebody for a while.

"Boats. I sleep over the shop." She tips her head at the shuttered window above the hatch. "Some nights, late, after the last lamp's out, there's oars. No lantern and no talking, just oars, slow, along under the quay toward the Seatower end. It comes back before first light." She frowns at the rag. "Goes out sitting low and comes back riding high. Like he's delivered something. I've heard it four, five times since the thaw. More, maybe. I don't get up to look, and I don't open the shutter."

She straightens, and the confiding is over as quickly as it started.

"There's a hundred warehouses on this harbour, master, and half of them have rats you can bargain with. Buy one of those." She sweeps his second copper into her apron. "That one's got a door nobody locks, and on this quay that means somebody doesn't need to."

A porter shoulders up to the hatch behind James, rattling coppers, and she turns to him without another word.

At James's boot the cat has heard all of it through him. Its tail wraps once around his ankle and stays there.

Over the water, the Seatower bell strikes the half hour. It's half past ten, and Brask won't be at the checkpoint until midday.

James lifts a hand to the alewife and leaves her to the porter.

He walks the quay the way the oars would go, toward the Seatower end, at the pace of a man stretching his legs after a beer. By late morning the waterfront is all elbows. A ship's crew is swaying a horse ashore in a sling while it screams about it. Two clerks argue over a manifest, and a fishwife sells eels out of a barrel to anyone who stands still long enough. The cat keeps its ten paces behind him, threading through ankles.

Where Pip's crate stood last night there's no crate, only a square of paler stone where it kept the rain off. James stops beside it and bends to fix a buckle that doesn't need fixing.

The crack is empty. A copper doesn't last a morning on this quay.

The cat puts its nose into the crack anyway. Through the link James gets old rain, a smear of tallow, a dozen boot soles, and very faintly Pip himself: cheap shaving soap and nervous sweat soaked into the stones where he sat. There's no deep salt in it, and no hand-warmed copper. Whatever was lying there last night was just a coin somebody dropped, and somebody else has picked it up. The cat sits back on its haunches and looks up at him. That's all there is.

He walks on.

Past the last lamppost the quay narrows and the crowd thins. By daylight the landing in front of the Seatower is a worn square of stone with a bollard and the iron mooring ring. The causeway runs out from its left side to the fortress, and the steps go down on the right. James stops at the top with his hands in the green coat's pockets and looks out at the ships riding at anchor, like a man adding up someone else's money. Out of the corner of his eye he looks at everything else.

The steps are easy to read. The tide is about halfway, and eight or nine steps show above the water. Below them, green weed sways in the brown harbour where more steps go on down. The weed-line on the quay wall stands as high as a man above the waterline. At low water the steps would run another eight feet down, and at high water the sea would be lapping two steps from the top.

The rest is harder to see from up here.

The quay face under him won't give up anything. From the top of the steps the stone drops away under his boots, and he can't see under the lip of the wall without leaning out over the water or going down, and he decided not to do either. The parts he can see are weed, barnacles and old mortar, the same as every yard of this harbour. There may be a hollow down there big enough to hide a skiff, or there may be nothing at all. He can't tell from up here, and he can't keep looking without becoming a man who stares at a wall.

The rest he can work out without leaning anywhere. The causeway parapet runs chest-high from the landing to the Seatower gate. Whoever stands guard at that gate faces along it, toward the city, and the parapet would hide the bottom of the steps from him. Up on the tower, the windows on this side are narrow slits set high, the kind built to shoot out of rather than look down from. In daylight a sentry up there could pick out a man on this landing. At night, past the last lamppost, with no lantern and a dark-painted boat, he'd see black water and nothing in it. The landing sits in the shadow of the Fist's own fortress, and it's the one place on the quay nobody would think to watch.

He looks at the ships a while longer, then turns back the way he came.

---

The cat stops on the way back.

The spot is a corner of a rope warehouse that they walked past going out, where a downpipe comes down the brick. James feels the cat go rigid before he sees it, and a stride later he gets what it smells. Wet wool that has dried and been soaked again. Lamp-black. The cold, clean salt of deep water.

It wasn't there an hour ago. The cat is sure of that, the way it's sure of everything it has already sorted. The smell is fresh, not days old like on the mooring ring or the Kettle's rail. Somebody stood at this corner since James went by, long enough to leave it on the brick at shoulder height, then went on.

The cat doesn't look around, because he taught it not to. It walks past the downpipe and catches up to his heel with its tail stiff as a stick. Behind them is the quay with its porters, its screaming horse, its eels and its clerks. No one in grey is in sight.

Across the water, the Seatower bell strikes the quarter past eleven.

---

The checkpoint looks different at midday. The trestle table is still there under the Flaming Fist banner, but a stout corporal with a cold in his nose holds the ledger, and the queue is half a dozen people off a river barge. James takes a seat on an empty fish crate against the harbourmaster's shed, where he can see the table, the quay, and the mouth of Cable Lane all at once. The cat settles under the crate in the shade, facing the way they came.

He waits three-quarters of an hour. Nothing grey turns up anywhere he can see.

The bells of the Lower City start striking noon from all their towers at once, out of step with each other. On the eighth stroke Brask comes up the quay from the causeway. She's in a clean tabard, her hair is still wet from a basin, and the oilcloth book makes a square shape under the red cloth at her ribs. She sees him on the crate before she reaches the table. Her eyes take in the green coat, then the soldier's cloak over it, then his face. She lets the corporal finish with a bargeman before she comes over, and she stops a short arm's length away, the same distance he kept from her last night.

"Worgen." She doesn't sit. "You didn't leave word with the keeper, so either you've nothing to tell me or you wanted to tell it to my face." She looks at the coat a moment longer. "Which is it?"

What he worked out about who can see the landing came from simple geometry, so that part didn't need a roll.*

He went there to answer one question: could a flat boat lie hidden under the lip of the quay, out of sight from above? He came away with no answer. The weed hung in the way, the angle from the top of the steps was wrong, and he wouldn't lean out or go down. So whatever is down there, a hollow or a culvert or plain wall, he still doesn't know. If he wants to find out, it will take another trip: from the water, or down the steps themselves, or at low tide when more of the wall shows.

"Forty paces," she says, to him and not to the water. "The tarred ones under canvas are salt-lighters. They've been laid up since before the thaw." She lets that sit for a moment. "Every boat on this harbour pays the harbourmaster mooring by the month, and his book says who pays. His book is Fist ground." That's all she says about it. Whatever she means to do with the book, she plans to do it when nobody is watching her do it.

When he picks Kettle's tonight and the steps tomorrow, she nods once.

"Tomorrow. Low water's nearer the second bell. Come to the dead-house an hour before and knock twice. Haskel won't open for one." Her eyes flick to his brow as the lazy salute comes up, then back. "He'll hear a line slip. He hears a rat change its mind."

She turns half toward the trestle table and lifts her voice to the flat, carrying pitch she uses for the queue.

"Next."

Anyone watching from the water sees a sellsword who asked about Fist work and got turned away.

---

James walks off without hurrying. He doesn't go up the quay toward the lighters. He goes back past the harbourmaster's shed and the eel barrel and turns in at the first lane, which climbs between a sailmaker's loft and a row of net-sheds. He takes two more turns he doesn't need, then a third, and comes out onto Cable Lane higher up, above the ropewalk, from the side nobody would expect.

The cat walks at his heel the whole way and doesn't look at the boats. Through the link he gets the afternoon street at ankle height: hemp dust, a dropped turnip, the tannery's smell rolling down from Tallow Lane, the sailmaker's beeswax. At every corner it sorts the air behind them, the way he taught it.

There's no deep salt in any of it, from either side. No wet wool, no lamp-black. Whoever was in the lighters didn't come off the water after him.

Halfway up Cable Lane, the cat stops at a doorstep and looks back the way they came, which it isn't supposed to do. It isn't looking at anything in the street. It's facing downhill, toward the quay and the harbour beyond the roofs, where a red tabard is still standing at a trestle table.

Then it turns around and catches up to his boot.

Behind the roofs the Seatower bell strikes the half hour. It's half past twelve, with the whole afternoon still ahead before the lamps.

*Out of game:* No roll this time. Nobody followed James off the quay, so the cat had nothing to catch. Kettle's opens after dark, and you owe Tansy 2 silver by lamplighting. What does James do with the afternoon?

turns.message:
I go on up Cable Lane to the blue door without stopping anywhere else.

If Tansy is about, I put two silver on the newel post where she'll see them. "Lamplighting came early. Remembered, not accounted."

Up in the top room I check the shutter first: is the scrap of card still wedged low between frame and sill, where I left it? Then the mattress, head and foot, for both bags, and the shadow behind the washbasin for the crossbow. If anything has moved, I want to know before I do anything else.

If it's all as I left it, I sit on the bed, take my papers out of the pack and spread them on the three-legged table, next to where the card case sat this morning. I've carried two of them since the south without really looking at them. The night I won, the promissory note was just money, and I put the letter from my old company away half-read because I didn't want what was in it. Now I'm in the city the Lady sent me to, a man has been watching me from a boat, and every name in Brask's book had a run of luck before the water took him.

So I read the promissory note properly this time: who signed it, for how much, drawn on whom, and payable where. Then I open the letter and read it to the end.

The cat can have the sill and the sun. *Watch the lane. I'm busy for a bit.*

When I'm done, I'll lie down for a couple of hours with my boots by the bed. Kettle's runs until two, low water's after that, and I want to be awake for both.
turns.reply:
The blue door is on the latch at this hour. Inside, Tansy sits at the kitchen table with a colander between her knees, shelling peas. She doesn't look up when the stairs creak under his boot. She looks up when two silver pieces click down on the newel post.

"Lamplighting came early," James says. "Remembered, not accounted."

Tansy looks at the coins and then out the window at the full daylight in the yard. "Lamplighting is when the lamps are lit. It isn't whenever a lodger gets bored." A pea pod snaps. She gets down off the stool anyway, walks to the post, picks up both coins and turns each one over before they go into her apron. "There. Now I've forgotten them." She goes back to the peas. "Don't track tar up my stairs."

---

The top room is warm under the roof, and it smells of hot slate and lavender.

He checks the shutter first. The folded card is still wedged low between the frame and the sill, at the same angle and the same depth, with the crease facing the room where he left it. He runs his hand under the head of the mattress and finds one bag, then under the foot and finds the other. Both are tied with the Counting House knot and neither looks lighter. Behind the washbasin the crossbow lies in the shadow of the pitch-mended crack with the bolts beside it, exactly as he put them down. Nobody has been in.

The cat jumps to the sill when he tells it to, folds itself into the strip of sun there and turns its ears toward the lane. Through the link come the ropewalk's hemp dust, the noon smell of frying onions from next door and a cart going downhill. It notices nothing it hasn't already sorted.

James sits on the bed and takes his papers out of the pack.

---

The promissory note is heavy paper, folded in three, and softer at the creases than it was a month ago. He opens it flat on the three-legged table and reads it properly for the first time.

The hand is careful and very young. Every letter is joined the way a tutor teaches it.

*On presentation, the Counting House of Baldur's Gate shall pay to the bearer three hundred gold pieces from the account of the House of Ammerstead. Given in good faith at the table, on the night written below.*

It is signed *Aurel Ammerstead*, with a flourish under the surname that wobbles at the end.

James holds the paper up to the light from the crack in the shutter. There is a watermark in the sheet, faint as breath: a shield, and on it a salt-cellar. Tansy laughed about those arms this morning. Nobody's allowed to laugh at them.

He remembers the hand that wrote this. It was soft and pale, with ink on the second finger and no calluses anywhere. A fair-haired young man of twenty or so sat across from him in that card room in the south. He gave only his first name and bet like someone who had never needed to count. On the last hand he pushed his stake in before he'd properly looked at his cards. At the time James had been busy praying and took it for nerves. Looking back with a gambler's eye, it doesn't sit right. The young man hadn't looked nervous. He'd looked like someone getting a thing over with. When he lost, he smiled and asked for paper.

James turns the note over. In the bottom corner of the back, in pencil and half smudged by a month in the pack, is a quick sketch: a woman's face, laughing with her head thrown back, and a coin held up between two of her fingers. It's only a few lines, the kind of thing a bored man draws while someone else is shuffling. He didn't notice it that night.

---

The letter is thinner, cheap paper, sealed once with a lump of candle wax that he broke a month ago and pressed shut again with his thumb. Halfway down the first side is the place where he stopped reading.

He reads it from the beginning.

*Jem,*

*Orso says you've left us for good this time. I'm not writing to call you back by the ear. You know where the company winters, and your place stays open until midsummer whether you come or not.*

*I'm writing because none of us said it to your face, and somebody should. We all saw where it was going. Every one of us watched you at those tables and kept quiet, because you're good company and you always paid your share in the end. That was cowardice on our part. I buried a man last winter for the dice, and I won't stand by the grave of a second one and say I didn't know.*

That's where he stopped a month ago. He keeps going.

*If you ever get out of the south, Wil Harrow, who carried the colours at Darromar, took the Flaming Fist's coin in Baldur's Gate. The last I heard he was a quartermaster at Wyrm's Rock. He'd stand you a drink. He wouldn't stand you a stake, so maybe that's the man to find.*

*Keep your head down and your hands where people can see them.*

*Ysolde.*

There's nothing else on it, not even a postscript.

---

He lays the two papers side by side on the table, where the card case sat this morning. Then he lies down on the lavender mattress with his boots by the bed and the rapier against the frame.

Sleep comes easier than he expected. The link carries the afternoon into it in small pieces: the ropewalk men calling the lengths, a barrow wheel that needs grease, Tansy's broom on the front step. At one point the half-eared tom comes along the ropewalk roof, sees who has the sill and sits down twelve feet below to wash, keeping his back to the window to show he hasn't noticed. Nobody stops under the window. There's no deep salt, no smoke and no wax.

When James opens his eyes, the strip of sun has moved off the sill and onto the wall above the washbasin, and it has gone the colour of late afternoon. Somewhere toward the market the bells are finishing a quarter past three. The cat is still at its post. When it feels him wake, it sends a single image of the tom's back with an opinion behind it.

The note and the letter lie where he left them.

---

*Out of game: the letter from your old company wasn't on James's record; only the pay slip and the promissory note were. I've treated it as backstory he's carried since the south and written what's in it. Tell me if you meant something different.*
